lessons.title: Narrative identity: is a life story what makes you the same self?
lessons.explanation: Lesson 74 asked which relation makes an earlier and a later person numerically the same person. This lesson raises a different question about the self. Grant that some continuity relation holds; what kind of thing is the self that relation is supposed to track? The narrative view answers that a person is partly constituted by the story she lives by. Marya Schechtman calls this the self-constitution view and separates two questions that are usually run together: the reidentification question, which asks what makes someone the same person over time, and the characterisation question, which asks what makes a set of actions and experiences belong to one person’s life at all. Her claim is that the characterisation question is answered by a narrative: a person is the subject of a life that is organised into an intelligible whole, with a past that explains a present and projects a future. Two further claims must be kept apart. The descriptive claim says that human beings in fact experience their lives narratively. The normative claim says we ought to live narratively, that a well-lived life takes the shape of a coherent story. Authors such as Alasdair MacIntyre and Charles Taylor press both; Paul Ricoeur frames narrative as the mediation between sameness and selfhood; Galen Strawson denies both. Whether narrativity is a fact about selves, a demand we place on them, or an optional temperament is contested, and this lesson keeps the three possibilities distinct.
lessons.example: Dara is fifty-two and left a medical degree at twenty-five to become a boat mechanic. Ask her why, and she gives an account that runs from a childhood spent repairing engines with her father, through a year of clinical work she describes as a mistake she had to make, to a present she finds meaningful. Notice what the account is doing. It is not a chronicle; it selects, orders, and assigns significance. Schechtman’s claim is that this ordering is not decoration added to a self that already exists. Without it, she argues, Dara would not be a single subject of a life at all, merely a sequence of states that a memory links only by association. Now add her friend Ravi, who describes himself in Strawson’s terms as episodic: he has memories, projects, and attachments, but no sense that they form a single unfolding story, and he resists being asked to produce one. The narrative view must say something about Ravi. If narrativity is constitutive, Ravi either has a narrative he does not notice or is a diminished self, which sounds harsh and possibly false. If narrativity is only an ideal, Ravi is a self who happens not to pursue it. Premise one: the self-constitution view gives a genuine explanation of why Dara’s past actions count as hers. Premise two: it appears to misdescribe or to downgrade people who genuinely live episodically. Both cannot be waved away, so the dispute turns on whether the constitutive claim survives the episodic counterexample.
lessons.question: According to Schechtman’s self-constitution view, what must a person’s self-narrative satisfy over and above being a story he can recount about himself?
lessons.answer: It must be substantially faithful to how his life actually goes, and one he can inhabit and endorse without self-deception
lessons.distractor: It must be a story that the people around him accept as an accurate portrait of who he is
lessons.correction: The reality constraint is about fit between the story and the life it organises, not about social agreement. A community’s endorsement is a separate proposal on which narrative identity is something others confer; that is a different view with different implications, and attributing it to Schechtman misstates her constraint.

depth.definitions: Narrative identity is the thesis that a person’s identity consists in, or is constituted by, an organised self-understanding rather than merely reported by it. Emplotment is the ordering of events into a sequence with significance, so that earlier elements explain later ones and later ones reinterpret earlier ones. A diachronic self experiences her life as extending through time with connected past and future; an episodic self, in Strawson’s sense, does not, though she may still plan and remember. The reality constraint says the narrative must track the actual course of the life rather than being a flattering fiction. Schechtman’s characterisation question asks what unifies the actions and experiences belonging to one life; her reidentification question asks the persistence question from lesson 74. Ricoeur’s idem/ipse contrast distinguishes sameness, the numerical and qualitative continuity of a thing, from selfhood, the reflexive relation a subject has to its own existence. Implicit in all of this is a prerequisite: you already need the concept of a person as a subject of experience before you can ask what constitutes one.
depth.mechanism: The view earns its place by explaining features that bare persistence conditions leave untouched. First, why actions from long ago are still yours to answer for even when your beliefs and character have changed: they belong to a life you are still the subject of, because the narrative you now hold interprets them and inherits their commitments. Second, why prudential concern for your distant future is normally rational, since that future is part of the same ongoing story rather than an unrelated stranger. Third, why certain kinds of damage to a life’s intelligibility, such as not being able to make sense of one’s own past, is felt as a loss of self rather than a loss of data. The pressure comes from three directions. The descriptive objection from Strawson is that many people simply do not experience their lives as narratives, so the constitutive claim is empirically overreaching. The epistemic objection notes that self-reports are reconstructive, that people confabulate explanations of their own choices, and that we should not build a metaphysical account on a faculty this unreliable; defenders reply that the reality constraint and the requirement of critical endorsement are precisely what disqualify a merely confabulated story. The normative objection holds that the demand for a coherent narrative can become an oppressive demand, valorising lives that look like a well-plotted novel and pathologising lives shaped by interruption, dependency, or trauma. How far the view can absorb these objections is not settled, and reasonable authors disagree about whether narrativity is a condition of selfhood, an ethical ideal, or neither.
depth.secondExample: Theo, a fictional composite, wakes from a head injury with intact vocabulary, competence, and an accurate set of documents describing his past, but no episodic memory of the years before the injury. He reads his old letters, hears testimony from his partner and his employer, and accepts the account: this was a man who took out a large loan to keep his parents’ shop open. Which verdict follows? On a psychological-continuity criterion the connection across the injury is severely attenuated, so the question of whether Theo is the same person who took the loan becomes pressing. On an animalist or biological criterion the organism persisted, so of course he is. On Schechtman’s narrative view the answer depends on whether Theo can integrate the documented history into an identity he can inhabit: testimony can supply narrative material, and nothing in the view requires that every element be first-personally remembered, but a story handed over wholesale that Theo cannot in any way own will not constitute a self. The philosophical payoff is that the narrative view can treat memory loss and identity-loss as capable of coming apart, which is exactly the distinction the pure memory criterion of lesson 74 was unable to make.
depth.mistake: The commonest error is to treat the narrative view as the trivially true observation that human beings can tell stories about themselves, or as the claim that any self-told story is as good as any other. Both misreadings collapse under the same test: ask what the story is doing. On the strong reading it does metaphysical work, constituting the subject rather than describing it, and it is constrained by the reality requirement, so a life organised around a false account of one’s own cruelty is not a well-constituted self but a self-deceived one. Diagnostics: a reader who says “everyone has a story, so nothing is at stake” has offered no argument; a reader who says “the narrative view makes identity a fiction” has ignored the reality constraint; a reader who says “narrative identity is just memory” has conflated two criteria that come apart in the Theo case.
depth.application: Non-blocking task. Take a real or fictional case in which a person publicly renounces an earlier commitment, for example leaving a religious order, repudiating a political affiliation, or refusing to keep supporting a relative. Produce a three-row table. Row one: the verdict of a psychological-continuity criterion, with the specific relation you are using. Row two: the verdict of Schechtman’s narrative view, including whether the renunciation is integrated into a revised narrative or merely announced. Row three: the verdict of a biological or animalist criterion. Then write two sentences stating which verdict you find most defensible and which objection or counterexample most threatens it. Model response: for the religious order case, psychological continuity usually yields that the later person is answerable for promises made at ordination because the beliefs, intentions, and memories form overlapping chains; the narrative view yields the same answer if the renunciation is narrated as a development that acknowledges what was owed, and a different answer if the earlier commitment is simply disowned and misdescribed; the animalist yields answerability without needing any of this, which is a strength in easy cases and an embarrassment in hard ones. Self-review rubric, four points: (1) the continuity relation is named, not gestured at; (2) the narrative verdict specifies whether the reality constraint is met; (3) the animalist row is not a straw man; (4) the stated objection is the strongest available, not the easiest.
depth.summary: Narrative identity is a claim about what constitutes a self, not merely about how people talk, and it buys explanatory power about promise-keeping, prudential concern, and the felt loss of self at the cost of a contested empirical and normative commitment. The transferable skill is to keep three questions apart in any identity dispute: which persistence criterion is being used, whether the unifying story tracks reality, and whether narrativity is being asserted as a fact, an ideal, or a mere preference. That discipline applies directly to how institutions treat people across time, from contracts and criminal responsibility to the care of people whose memories or self-understandings have been disrupted.

readings.title: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, ‘Paul Ricoeur’ — section 5, ‘Narrative Identity and the Turn to Selfhood’
readings.note: Section 5 is the canonical short exposition of narrative identity and of the idem/ipse distinction, and states how Ricoeur connects narrative to ethics and to memory. visual.title: From a sequence of states to a narrated self, and the three objections
visual.description: Show a timeline of a life with events, then show the ordering and significance that a narrative imposes on those events, and mark three points where critics attack the move.
steps: Raw sequence: events, actions, and experiences arranged only by date, with no significance assigned
Emplotment: the same events reordered causally and evaluatively so earlier ones explain later ones and later ones reinterpret earlier ones
Constitution: the self is identified with the organised self-understanding, subject to the reality constraint that it must fit how the life actually goes
Objection 1 (descriptive): episodic lives exist, so narrativity is not a universal fact
Objection 2 (epistemic): self-reports are reconstructive, so the organising story may be confabulated
Objection 3 (normative): the demand for coherence can pathologise interrupted or dependent lives

lessons.title: The hard problem of consciousness: statement, challenge, and the illusionist reply
lessons.explanation: Lesson 76 mapped dualism, physicalism, and the explanatory gap as positions. This lesson works a single argument in detail: the hard problem, as David Chalmers formulated it. The distinction he draws is between the easy problems and the hard problem of consciousness. Easy problems concern the function and mechanism of cognitive capacities: how information is discriminated, integrated, and used to guide behaviour, how attention selects, how a system reports its own states. They are hard science, but in principle they are answered by specifying a mechanism that performs the function. The hard problem is why the performance of any such function is accompanied by subjective experience, by something it is like for the system itself. On Chalmers’s account this question is not answered by further detail about function, because no amount of information about what a system does tells us why there is something it is like to be that system. He then considers reductive strategies, including functional explanation and nonreductive explanation, and argues that each either explains a related capacity or simply posits experience alongside physical processes. His own proposal introduces experience as a fundamental feature governed by additional bridging principles, which he presents as a research programme rather than a solution. The interlocutor to keep in view is the deflationary one. Daniel Dennett and Keith Frankish argue that the hard problem rests on an intuition that will not survive scrutiny: what Chalmers treats as an unassailable datum is, on the illusionist account, a representation of an experience that is not itself as it seems. The honest summary is that both the existence and the tractability of the hard problem are contested, and that neither side has carried the day.
lessons.example: Take a hypothetical system, an artificial network that reliably detects heat, withdraws its probe, and reports a temperature. Ask two questions about it. The easy question: what mechanism explains the detection, the withdrawal, and the report? Here we expect a functional answer in terms of sensors, weights, and outputs, and if the system also monitors its own states and makes them available to further processing, that is still a functional story about access. The hard question: is there anything it is like to be this system while it does all this? Notice the structure of the argument that follows. Premise one: for every capacity described in functional terms, a complete functional account is available in principle; nothing in the specification of detection, withdrawal, or reporting leaves a gap in the functional story. Premise two: the fact of subjective experience, if there is one here, is not entailed by any such functional account, because a functionally identical system that behaved identically is conceivable and would not, by hypothesis, be conscious. Conclusion: if experience exists, it is something over and above the functional facts. This is the conceivability-to-possibility route familiar from the zombie thought experiment, and it is exactly where the debate concentrates. A physicalist replies that this argument proves at most a fact about our concepts, not about the world: we can conceive of the functional duplicate because our concept of experience is not a functional concept, but inconceivability does not follow from failure of imagination. A defender of the hard problem replies that the gap is not a gap in our concepts but in our explanatory practice: it is not that we cannot imagine the identity, it is that no deduction of experience from structure is on offer, and, unlike the case of water and H2O, we cannot say what the identity would even be doing.
lessons.question: Why does Chalmers hold that further progress on the easy problems of consciousness, even complete success in explaining cognitive functions, would not by itself resolve the hard problem?
lessons.answer: Because the easy problems ask what a system does, while the hard problem asks why doing any of it is accompanied by subjective experience, which functional explanation appears to leave untouched
lessons.distractor: Because the easy problems are not yet solved empirically, so we cannot know whether a functional account will eventually cover experience as well
lessons.correction: Chalmers’s claim is not a prediction about future data collection but a structural claim about the kind of explanation that functional accounts provide. Treating the hard problem as a temporary empirical gap is precisely the reductive strategy he targets; you may accept that strategy, but you should see that you are disagreeing with him rather than describing his view.

depth.definitions: Phenomenal consciousness is the subjective, qualitative aspect of experience, contrasted with access consciousness, which concerns a state’s availability for reasoning, control, and report. The easy problems are the functional questions: how capacities are implemented and what they do. The hard problem is the question of why any of that is accompanied by phenomenal character. A zombie, in the philosophical sense, is an imagined being physically and functionally identical to a normal person but lacking phenomenal experience. The explanatory gap is the apparent impossibility of deducing phenomenal facts from physical facts, as distinct from the mere fact that a particular reduction has not yet been accomplished. Illusionism is Frankish’s version of the deflationary reply: the phenomenal character we seem to find in introspection is a representation, and the thing represented does not exist. The meta-problem is the question of why we think and say that there is a hard problem, which illusionists hold is the tractable target. Prerequisite concept from lesson 76: the causal closure of the physical and the interaction problem for dualist proposals.
depth.mechanism: The hard problem generates its force by a contrast between paradigms of successful explanation. In the standard model, an explanation succeeds by showing that the phenomenon is identical with, or a consequence of, lower-level structure: water is H2O, temperature is mean molecular kinetic energy, and once the identification is established, no further question remains about what the thing really is. Applied to consciousness, the identification would need a bridge from structure and function to phenomenal character, and Chalmers argues that any such bridge must be simply posited. That is why he treats experience as fundamental and offers bridging principles, in the way physics treats charge or mass as fundamental and offers laws relating them. Three responses are live. The first accepts a version of the hard problem and revises metaphysics, as Russellian monism and panpsychist proposals do by locating experience in the intrinsic nature of the physical rather than in its structure. The second denies that anything needs explaining in Chalmers’s sense, on the illusionist ground that introspective acquaintance with a non-functional quality is itself a cognitive phenomenon to be explained. The third, the phenomenal-concept strategy, keeps physicalism and argues that the gap is an artefact of the concepts we use to think about experience, so that zombies are conceivable only insofar as we lack the concepts that would render the identity transparent. Each response buys its resolution at a price: panpsychism pays in the combination problem of how micro-experiences compose into a subject, illusionism pays by denying what many take to be the one datum they cannot doubt, and the phenomenal-concept strategy risks proving only that we are ignorant rather than that physicalism is true. That trade-off, not a settled answer, is the state of the debate, and it is worth stating plainly that no proposal currently commands general acceptance.
depth.secondExample: Consider the contrast with a reduction that succeeded, and with one that stalled for a different reason. Vitalism once held that living processes required a special force, because mechanical chemistry was thought unable to produce reproduction, growth, and metabolism. That posited force was not refuted by an argument about conceivability; it was displaced as biochemistry explained the functions, and nobody now thinks an extra ingredient is needed. The hard-problem controversy is whether consciousness will follow the vitalism path or whether it is structurally different. A second contrast sharpens the point. Lightning was once explained by appeal to divine will, and the modern account replaced it with a mechanism. In the lightning case the replacement left no residue; nobody asks why the mechanism is accompanied by lightning over and above the discharge. If consciousness is like lightning, illusionism is vindicated and the residual question dissolves. If it is unlike lightning, the residue is a genuine datum and the hard problem stands. The decision between these readings cannot be made by pointing to the success of reduction elsewhere; it turns on whether the residual question is a question with an answer, and that is exactly what the disputants disagree about.
depth.mistake: Two symmetric mistakes are common. The first is to treat the hard problem as a solved matter in either direction: to announce that consciousness has been explained or that it has been proved physically irreducible. The first overstates the deflationary case, since illusionism is a substantive and contested thesis rather than a settled result about introspection; the second overstates the gap, since an epistemic gap does not by itself establish a metaphysical one. The second mistake is to confuse the explanatory gap with the claim that dualism is true. Diagnostics: ask the writer which premise the conclusion needs, whether it is about what we can conceive or about what exists, and whether the argument would still go through if the phenomenal-concept strategy were correct. A paragraph that survives those three questions is doing philosophy; one that does not is asserting a verdict it has not argued for.
depth.application: Non-blocking task. Select one proposal from the four reviewed above, namely the identity-theory-plus-phenomenal-concepts strategy, illusionism, Russellian monism or panpsychism, and Chalmers’s fundamental-property programme. Write an assessment with exactly four parts: (1) the proposal stated in two sentences as a claim about what exists; (2) the single strongest argument for it, in premise form; (3) the strongest objection to it, with the objection traced to one premise; (4) a verdict that states what you take to be unresolved. Model response, for illusionism: (1) what we report when we report a phenomenal quality is a representation produced by introspective attention, and the represented quality does not exist as represented; (2) millions of introspective judgments about mental life have turned out to be systematically mistaken, and this one has features of the previous cases, such as resistance to third-person correction; (3) objection: the thesis appears self-undermining, since it must describe the illusion without invoking an experienced appearance, and no formulation is agreed; verdict: unresolved, because the objection depends on contested claims about how to describe appearances. Self-review rubric: (1) the proposal is stated as a claim about existence rather than about vocabulary; (2) the argument is in premise form with an identifiable weakest link; (3) the objection targets a premise rather than asserting a contrary view; (4) the verdict distinguishes what is known from what is contested.
depth.summary: The hard problem is a claim about the limits of a particular style of explanation, and it stands or falls with whether the residual question about experience is genuine. You now have the tools to work any version of it: state the easy/hard contrast, identify whether an argument moves from conceivability to possibility or from explanatory failure to metaphysical conclusion, and price each proposed resolution honestly. The transferable habit is to look for the residue that a successful explanation leaves behind, because that residue, and not the number of empirical details, is what a debate about consciousness is actually about.

visual.title: Easy problems, the hard problem, and the four responses
visual.description: Show a functional description of a system on one side and the question of subjective experience on the other, then lay out how each position attempts to close or deny the distance between them.
steps: Easy problems: discrimination, integration, report, attention — each answered by specifying a mechanism that performs the function
Hard problem: why the performance of any such function is accompanied by something it is like to be the system
Response A, fundamental-property programme: experience is basic, bridging principles relate it to physical structure
Response B, Russellian monism or panpsychism: experience is the intrinsic nature of the physical, with a remaining combination problem
Response C, illusionism: the felt quality is a representation, so the meta-problem is the target
Response D, phenomenal concept strategy: the gap is an artefact of our concepts, so physicalism is preserved

lessons.title: Responsibility as a practice: reactive attitudes, excuses, and standing
lessons.explanation: Lesson 75 treated free will as a metaphysical question about whether an action originates in the agent. This lesson treats responsibility as a social practice and asks what that practice presupposes. The shift is P. F. Strawson’s, in ‘Freedom and Resentment’. Strawson observes that we do not merely register that someone did something; we respond to it in person-directed ways. These responses, which he calls reactive attitudes, include resentment at injury, indignation on behalf of others, gratitude, hurt, love, and forgiveness. They are not conclusions we infer from a theory of agency; they are expressions of our involvement with one another, and they are essential to it. When we cannot respond in this way we take what Strawson calls the objective stance: we treat the person as a case to be understood, managed, or treated. Ordinary cases of illness, immaturity, or incapacity move us partly toward that stance, and the important point is that the two stances are different relations to a person, not degrees of the same thing. Strawson then reframes the free-will debate. The optimist says our practices survive the truth of determinism; the pessimist says they cannot; the sceptic says the notions are incoherent. Strawson’s proposal is that the dispute is misconceived when it is run as an inference from a metaphysical thesis, and that the practices rest on our natural involvement rather than on a theoretical belief. He does not claim to refute the pessimist. The result is a widely used framework and a contested one: it is now standard to distinguish, following Gary Watson, the attributability of an action to an agent, which is about what the action reveals of her, from accountability, which concerns what others may legitimately demand of her, and to recognise that blame requires standing as well as warrant.
lessons.example: A colleague, Ana, publishes a comment mocking a paper of yours, and you resent it. Strawson’s framework organises the many ways that response could be modified. First, excuses, which bear on the act without withdrawing the participant stance: Ana was misinformed about what your paper argued, so the comment was not an expression of contempt; her assistant posted it under her name by mistake, so it was not her action at all. Notice that these defeat the particular reactive attitude without implying Ana is not a party to interpersonal relations. Second, exemptions, which do withdraw that stance: if Ana were, in a relevant way, not a competent participant in these relations, resentment would be out of place in a different manner, and the appropriate response would become something like management or care rather than indignation. Third, standing, a condition on the holder of the attitude rather than on the agent: suppose you have spent years anonymously mocking the work of others, or suppose Ana is a subordinate whose career you control. Your resentment may be understandable and still not carry the force of blame, because blame retains some of the meaning of a demand made between parties whose footing is equal. Fourth, a definitional question about the attitude itself: is your response personal resentment or impersonal indignation on behalf of the discipline? Strawson treats these as related but distinct, and the distinction matters because a third party’s standing is different from a victim’s. Working through the four levels is the analytical skill this lesson teaches: the same act can warrant one reactive attitude and not another, and ‘is she responsible?’ is too blunt a question to capture that.
lessons.question: In Strawson’s framework, what distinguishes an excuse from an exemption when we assess an agent who has caused harm?
lessons.answer: An excuse defeats the particular reactive attitude by changing the description of the act, while an exemption withdraws the participant stance altogether
lessons.distractor: An excuse concerns factual mistakes about what happened, while an exemption concerns whether harm actually occurred
lessons.correction: The distinction is not about the facts of the incident but about the relation between the parties. A mistaken belief about what someone did can excuse an attitude while leaving the person fully a participant in interpersonal relations; an exemption, by contrast, modifies the relation itself, so blame gives way to management or care rather than to a corrected version of the same response.

depth.definitions: Reactive attitudes are person-directed responses such as resentment, indignation, gratitude, and forgiveness, which Strawson treats as constitutive of interpersonal relations rather than as conclusions derived from a theory. The participant stance is the relation we occupy when we hold someone responsible in this way; the objective stance treats her as an object of explanation, management, or treatment. An excuse defeats an attitude by altering the description of the action, as when it was accidental or coerced. An exemption withdraws the participant stance by denying the agent’s competence as a participant in the relevant relations. Optimism holds that our practices do not require the falsity of determinism; pessimism holds that they do; scepticism denies that the notions of guilt and responsibility make sense at all. Attributability is the connection between an action and what it reveals about the agent; accountability is the relation that licenses demands, blame, and sanctions. Standing is a condition on the blamer, not on the blamed. Prerequisite from lesson 75: the leeway and sourcehood conditions, since Strawson’s real target is the assumption that either condition is what our practices are about.
depth.mechanism: Why does this reframing change the shape of the argument? Because it replaces a single question about a metaphysical thesis with a set of questions about a practice and its internal conditions. If responsibility is a practice of demand and response, then what could undermine it is not an abstract thesis but the demonstration that the participants are not what the practice takes them to be. That is why Strawson’s reply to the pessimist is not a proof that determinism is compatible with responsibility; it is the claim that the pessimist over-intellectualises, treating the practice as resting on a belief that could be argued out of us. The framework has real costs, and they are contested. First, the naturalistic account threatens to make existing blaming practices unrevisable: if the attitudes are simply natural, then a society that blames victims, or that punishes disproportionately, can describe its practices the same way, and a standard criticism holds that a descriptive naturalism gives us too little leverage to condemn them. Second, the distinction between attributability and accountability raises the possibility that an action can reveal something about a person, and be genuinely hers, while no one has the standing to make a demand about it, which splits responsibility claims that were once treated as one. Third, the conversational and forward-looking approaches that grew out of this literature replace the question of whether an agent deserved an attitude with the question of what the practice of holding responsible is for, and those two questions can pull apart, notably in cases of profound moral deprivation, where an agent was raised without access to the considerations that would make a demand intelligible.
depth.secondExample: Apply the framework to punishment rather than to a private attitude, and then to a case of no personal victim. In a criminal case, the state claims not resentment but a license to impose hard treatment, and on Strawson’s picture its authority has to be grounded in the same interpersonal relation rather than in a separate argument from consequences; this is why so much of the debate about criminal justice turns on whether the relevant attitudes are impersonal indignation or something else again. Now consider a case with no victim at all: an engineer who signs off on a safety assessment she has not read, in a project that happens never to fail. Nothing is harmed, yet the act is attributable to her, and a supervisor’s criticism expresses a demand about how work is to be done. A consequentialist framing struggles here, since no bad outcome occurred to deter; the reactive-attitude framing explains why criticism is apt, because the practice concerns what agents may be demanded to do, not only what they have caused. Now vary the case so that the same engineer is criticised by a colleague who routinely signs off without reading. Nothing about the first engineer’s act changes, but the standing of the critic does, which shows that the warrant for an attitude and the right to express it are separate conditions that must be checked independently.
depth.mistake: The dominant misconception is that Strawson provides a compatibilist proof, so that a reader concludes ‘Strawson showed determinism is irrelevant to responsibility’ and stops. He does not establish that; he changes the subject from a metaphysical premise to the conditions internal to a practice, and a convinced pessimist or hard incompatibilist can accept that description and still argue that the practice should be revised or abandoned. Diagnostic questions: does your paragraph state whether you are making a claim about what the practice is or about what it ought to be? If it asserts that the practices are vindicated, which argument does that conclusion rest on? A second, subtler error is to treat the objective stance as the correct or scientific stance and the participant stance as its confused predecessor, which inverts Strawson’s point that the two are different relations, each appropriate in its domain, rather than a correct view and an error.
depth.application: Non-blocking task. Construct a responsibility audit for a scenario you devise, in which an agent causes a significant harm through negligence. Your audit must list: (1) the action’s description as it would be framed by the careful observer, noting any factual defeater; (2) the reactive attitudes that would be apt from a victim, from a third party, and from someone with authority over the agent’s work; (3) any exemption claim and what exactly it alleges about the agent’s competence as a participant; (4) the standing of each potential blamer, with the specific reason; (5) one forward-looking alternative, such as a demand, a training requirement, or a sanction, stating what it is for. Model response for a case in which a laboratory supervisor fails to review a safety log: (1) the act is the omission of a review she was contracted to perform, not the mere existence of the hazard; (2) a technician who was injured may resent; a colleague may express impersonal indignation on behalf of the standard; a regulator may act without resentment at all; (3) a claim that she was working a double shift and lacked the capacity to review does not exempt her, since capacity in this sense is the ordinary capacity to perform the role, so it functions as an excuse for the particular lapse if anything; (4) the colleague has standing only if the standard binds both; (5) a forward-looking response is to require independent sign-off, justified by the risk it removes rather than by her desert. Rubric, four points: (1) the action is described rather than labelled; (2) apt attitudes are distinguished by holder; (3) the exemption claim is tested against the notion of a participant rather than reduced to a factual excuse; (4) the forward-looking alternative states its aim.
depth.summary: Responsibility is analysed here as a practice with internal conditions: an attitude, an apt target, a competent participant, and a blamer with standing. This shifts the free-will dispute from a single metaphysical question to a set of questions about what our practices presuppose and whether they can be revised, and it exposes the distinction between what an action reveals about a person and what others may demand of her. Carry forward the habit of asking, for any responsibility claim, which condition is doing the load-bearing work, since that habit transfers directly to the next lesson, where the disputed condition is the agent’s history rather than her present capacities.

visual.title: Four conditions on a responsibility claim
visual.description: Show a single harmful act and four separate questions that must be answered before blame is warranted, with the distinct way each one can fail.
steps: Act description: what was done, so that excuses can defeat the particular attitude
Attitude type: personal resentment, impersonal indignation, or a demand made by an institution
Participant competence: whether an exemption applies, moving us toward the objective stance of management or care
Standing of the blamer: whether this person may make the demand, given hypocrisy, complicity, or unequal power

Forward-looking alternative: what the practice of holding responsible is for, stated separately from what the agent deserves

lessons.title: Manipulation and personal history: does how you got this way affect what you deserve?
lessons.explanation: Lesson 75 introduced the manipulation problem in passing. Here it becomes the main argument. The question is whether responsibility depends not only on what an agent is like and does at the moment of acting, but also on how she came to be that way. The most systematic statement is Derk Pereboom’s four-case argument, which runs a single case through four versions. In case one, a team of neuroscientists implants a device that makes Professor Plum decide to commit a murder; Plum deliberates, reasons as he always has, and acts, and we are to agree that he is not responsible. In case two, the manipulation occurred at birth, so that Plum’s character and reasoning dispositions were engineered from the start; the details are deterministic, and we are invited to agree that the outcome is still not his responsibility. In case three, a community intentionally designs Plum’s upbringing to produce a ruthless practical reasoner of exactly this kind; the manipulation is now ordinary environmental influence, deliberately arranged, and the agreement is meant to still hold. In case four, Plum’s ruthless dispositions and his insensitivity to others’ interests are the product of an ordinary upbringing in a society with a history of oppression and no one planned anything. The argument holds that there is no difference in responsibility-relevant features between cases three and four, so if Plum is not responsible in the first three he is not responsible in the fourth either, and since ordinary humans are, by hypothesis, in case four, ordinary humans are not responsible. The compatibilist must either find a relevant difference among the cases, which is the soft-line reply, or explain why our confident judgments about the first cases should be revised rather than extended, which is the hard-line reply.
lessons.example: Two agents are identical at the moment of the crime, call them Ivy and Ivy*. Ivy* carries a covert implant installed in infancy that guarantees she will reason ruthlessly and defect from her partner when the opportunity arises; Ivy has exactly the same character, formed by an upbringing that, as it happens, was engineered by no one. Each deliberates, each acts for reasons she fully accepts, and neither would have done otherwise. If you hold that Ivy* is not responsible, what exactly are you claiming? Not that she was coerced at the time, since she was not; not that she lacked reasons-responsiveness, since by stipulation she has it; not that she was unaware of the significance of her action, since she understands it perfectly. You are claiming that the causal origin of her reasons-responsiveness defeats responsibility, and that origin is the only respect in which her case differs from Ivy’s. Now put pressure on the claim from the other side. Suppose the implant is disclosed after the fact, and Ivy* is told that the person she is was designed by others. Is her sense that her action was nonetheless hers simply an illusion, or is it a datum the manipulation argument must accommodate? Pereboom’s case two and case three are designed to make the difference between engineered and environmental origins look like a difference in the story rather than a difference in the agent. His opponents argue that the intuitive pull of case one proves less than he needs, because the standard example smuggles in features we would object to anyway, such as a first-order desire the agent would reject if she attended to it, and those features are what ground the non-responsibility judgment, not the manipulation as such.
lessons.question: Pereboom’s four-case argument asks us to extend a verdict about a manipulated agent to ordinary agents. What does it claim licenses that extension?
lessons.answer: That the first three cases and the ordinary case do not differ in any feature relevant to responsibility, only in the causal history by which the agent’s dispositions were produced
lessons.distractor: That ordinary agents are manipulated by social institutions in the same coercive sense as an implanted agent, so coercion is present in both
lessons.correction: The argument does not rest on there being coercion in ordinary cases. Its force comes from a parity premise: the features we would normally cite as making an agent answerable, such as deliberation, reasons-responsiveness, and understanding of the act, are stipulated to be present in the manipulated cases too. The contest is whether the parity premise is true, which is why replies divide into those that find a difference and those that challenge the starting verdict.

depth.definitions: A manipulation argument concludes that ordinary agents are not responsible by comparing them with agents whose histories are rigged, on the ground that no responsibility-relevant feature distinguishes the two. Bypassing names the charge that in manipulation cases the action fails to flow from the agent’s own evaluative capacities, as it does in ordinary action. Hard incompatibilism is Pereboom’s position: responsibility of the desert-entailing kind is incompatible with both determinism and indeterminism, so it should be given up, though forward-looking practices such as protection, moral exhortation, and reform are retained. Sourcehood is the condition that an action must issue from the agent appropriately, in contrast to leeway, the condition that she could have done otherwise. Reasons-responsiveness is the capacity to recognise and respond to reasons, discussed in lesson 75 as a leading compatibilist criterion. Historical compatibilism makes the acquisition history of an agent’s capacities relevant, whereas structural or time-slice accounts assess only the agent as she is at the moment of action. The zygote argument, due to Alfred Mele, is a compact cousin of the four cases in which a designer arranges a zygote so that it will develop into a thief.
depth.mechanism: The argument works by removing everything a compatibilist might point to, case by case, so that the only remaining variable is causal origin. Its structure is a parity premise plus a transfer premise: the verdict of non-responsibility transfers from the early cases to the later ones because no relevant difference separates them. Replies therefore have exactly two targets. Soft-line replies claim a difference: in the manipulated cases the agent’s reasoning is severed from her own history of evaluating reasons, or she lacks the ordinary standing to demand better treatment from others, or her action is not responsive to reasons in the way that matters because the responsiveness was installed rather than developed. Hard-line replies accept that there is no deep difference and argue that the intuition about the early cases is the mistaken term in the equation; a compatibilist may hold that a fully reasons-responsive, deliberating agent who endorses her action is responsible, and that our queasiness about the implant reflects an unprincipled horror at manipulation rather than a principle about agency. The costs are symmetric. Soft-line replies must specify the difference precisely enough that it does not collapse into a bare appeal to naturalness, since much of what shapes any of us is not chosen. Hard-line replies must explain why our judgment about the radical cases is so confident, and they give up the intuition that being made to be a certain way is exculpating, which some find counterintuitive in the extreme. Whether either reply succeeds is unresolved, and the literature continues to generate cases designed to break particular replies.
depth.secondExample: The same structure appears in a case of praise, and the comparison is informative. Consider a person whose extraordinary generosity is the product of a deliberate, benevolent programme of upbringing, with no effort or choice of her own in acquiring it. If the argument transfers, our admiration is also misplaced, since the same parity reasoning applies; if praise is retained because it registers what the agent has become and expresses an invitation to continue, the symmetry between blame and praise can be broken. A second contrast concerns inaction and inherited attitudes. Suppose an agent fails to notice that a policy excludes a group, because everyone in her professional circle treats the exclusion as normal, and she has never had occasion to consider it. Nothing about her deliberation is defective by the standards of her environment, and yet the exclusion continues. Here the manipulation framework morphs into the question of responsibility for unreflective participation in unjust structures, and the honest observation is that both the frameworks of lessons 75 and 83 and the manipulation argument are being asked to do work they were not designed for: the first two concern individual agency, while the third concerns the allocation of responsibility for patterns no one agent brings about.
depth.mistake: The usual error is to treat the parity premise as obviously false because one can always name a difference, for instance that in the manipulated cases someone else intended the outcome. Intending the outcome is a fact about the engineer, not about Plum, and a difference that lies only in another person’s intentions does not show that Plum’s responsibility-relevant features differ; the reply must show the manipulation changes what the agent does or is. The opposite error is to treat the argument as knocking down compatibilism single-handedly. It is one argument, it depends on a contested verdict about the early cases, and the hard-line reply is live. Diagnostic: for any objection, ask whether it attacks the parity premise or the verdict about case one, because an objection that attacks neither is not yet addressed to the argument.
depth.application: Non-blocking task. Take the four Pereboom cases and produce a table with one row per case and four columns: (1) your verdict on responsibility and whether it is full, partial, or absent; (2) the single feature you cite as doing the work; (3) whether that feature is present in case four; (4) if you judge case four differently, whether you are therefore a soft-liner seeking a difference or a hard-liner rejecting the verdict in case one. Then write three sentences on what would have to be true for your row-four judgment to be stable. Model response for a soft-line verdict: case one, not responsible, feature is that the agent’s practical reasoning was bypassed by an engineer’s intervention on her evaluative states in a way that made the action not expressive of her; case four, responsible, because the same feature is absent since no one intervened, and the historical conditions that formed her need not bypass her own practical reasoning; the concession is that a case in which the bypassing is total from birth, which is Pereboom’s case two, is the hardest for this reply. Rubric: (1) the verdict is stated rather than implied; (2) the cited feature is a fact about the agent, not about the manipulator; (3) the table is consistent, so that if the feature appears in case four you do not conclude non-responsibility; (4) the closing sentences identify the vulnerability of your own view rather than a vulnerability of the other side.
depth.summary: The manipulation argument pushes responsibility claims backward in time, asking whether it matters how an agent became the way she is, and it forces a choice between finding a difference among the cases and giving up the verdict the argument starts from. The skill to retain is the diagnosis of which premise an objection targets, since the same habit resolves disputes about implicit bias, about inherited advantage, and about punishment, where appeals to history and appeals to present competence regularly talk past one another.

Case 2: intervention at the origin of the agent’s character — non-responsibility claimed to transfer
Case 3: deliberate environmental design of upbringing — non-responsibility claimed to transfer

lessons.title: Normative reasons and rationality: internalism, externalism, and the wrong kind of reason
lessons.explanation: When we say someone had a reason to act, we may mean one of two very different things. A motivating reason is the consideration for which she acted: the fact that she took the train was because her sister was unwell, and that fact figured in her deliberation. A normative reason is a consideration that counts in favour of acting, whether or not it moves anyone. The distinction is not verbal. A person can act on a consideration that does not really favour the action, and a consideration can favour an action that no one is moved by. The central dispute in this area is whether normative reasons must be able to connect to an agent’s actual motivation. Bernard Williams gives the classic internalist answer: a reason for an agent to act must be reachable by sound deliberation from her subjective motivational set, the collection of her desires, commitments, loyalties, projects, and evaluative attitudes. If nothing in that set could be brought by reasoning to favour the action, then, Williams argues, there is no reason for her to act, and any theory that says otherwise is committed to reasons that could not explain anything, including the actions they are supposed to justify. Externalists such as Derek Parfit and Thomas Scanlon reply that this makes reasons hostage to the psychology of whoever happens to be considering the question, and that claims like ‘her future suffering matters, so she has reason to take the medicine whether or not she cares’ seem true as stated. A distinct puzzle concerns the kind of reason: a threat can make it the case that you have some reason to do something that is in no way worth doing, which is why reasons of the wrong kind must be separated from reasons grounded in the value of the object.
lessons.example: Williams’s gin-and-tonic case isolates the internalist’s structure. A thirsty man is offered a glass he believes to contain gin and tonic and reaches for it; the liquid is in fact petrol. Does he have a reason to drink it? He believes he does, and he is motivated, but the internalist says no: once his false belief about the contents is corrected, nothing in his motivational set, now combined with true beliefs, favours drinking petrol. His state before the correction gives him a reason to do something, but the description under which it has motivating force is different from the description under which he acts. Compare the same man an hour later, when he has been told the truth and is offered a glass of actual gin. Now his desire for gin, plus true beliefs about the contents, yields a normative reason to drink. Then compare a third variant: he is told the liquid is a medicine that will prevent a future illness he cares very much about avoiding. The reason now comes from a commitment already in his set. To make the case a genuine test between the positions, add a person who simply does not care about his own future health at all. The externalist says he nevertheless has reason to take the medicine, because his future suffering is bad for him; the internalist says that if nothing in his set would yield concern, the claim that he has reason is an assertion whose motivating force cannot be explained, and notice that the externalist owes an account of what makes the claim true without appeal to any such force. Set out that way, the dispute is not about whether reasons motivate, since both sides grant that normative reasons are often motivating. It is about whether being capable of motivating is part of what a reason is.
lessons.question: Why does Williams hold that the man reaching for the glass in the gin-and-tonic example has no normative reason to drink, even though he is thirsty and believes it contains gin?
lessons.answer: Because sound deliberation from his actual motivational set, corrected for his false belief, gives nothing that favours drinking what is in the glass
lessons.distractor: Because petrol is harmful, and harmful consequences cannot form part of a reason for a rational agent
lessons.correction: The verdict does not rest on the harmfulness of petrol. Williams’s internalism makes the reason depend on the reachability of the consideration from the agent’s motivations; that is why the externalist can accept the harmfulness claim and still deny his conclusion. Identifying the harmfulness as the engine of the argument confuses an externalist consideration with the internalist structure of the example.

depth.definitions: A normative reason is a consideration that counts in favour of an attitude or action; a motivating reason is the consideration for which someone in fact acted; explanatory reasons are whatever explains a piece of behaviour, which may be a cause that is not a reason at all. The subjective motivational set in Williams’s sense contains much more than appetites: it includes dispositions of evaluation, patterns of emotional reaction, personal loyalties, and projects, so internalism is not the view that we are pushed around by desires. Sound deliberation is the procedure by which elements of the set are combined with true beliefs to yield conclusions about what to do. Internalism about reasons holds that a reason must be reachable from such a set; externalism denies this. The wrong kind of reason problem is that some considerations, such as threats and rewards, appear to give reasons for attitudes even though they do not bear on the object of the attitude. Structural rationality concerns coherence among attitudes, for example between an intention and a belief about the means, while substantive rationality concerns the justification of the ends themselves. Prerequisite from lesson 74 onwards: the contrast between a criterion applied to a case and the theory that the criterion is meant to serve, since every example below is doing that work.
depth.mechanism: Internalism is pressed by a motivational argument. If a normative reason could not move the agent, then a reason statement cannot play the explanatory role we expect of it, namely the role of making the action intelligible; and since reason statements are used to explain and to advise, a doctrine that severs reasons from motivation renders its own language idle. Williams adds the further thought that external reasons carry an implausible demand: they tell an agent to be moved by something that is not, as a matter of his psychology, capable of moving him. Externalism is pressed by extensional arguments, which exhibit cases in which we are strongly inclined to say the reason exists regardless of the agent’s set, such as a person who does not care about her own coming suffering, or an agent who has been raised to be indifferent to a requirement of morality. A technical objection, the conditional fallacy, cuts in the other direction against an internalism that is stated too crudely: the analysis ‘A has a reason to act if she would be moved after sound deliberation’ can be satisfied by an agent whose set is transformed by the very deliberation that was supposed to operate on it, so that the conditional attributes a reason on the basis of a change that would have removed the original motive. The most defensible internalisms therefore relativise to how the agent would be after correct deliberation without assuming she can always reach the reason rather than acquiring it. Where the debate stands is genuinely contested: the modal question of whether reasons depend on agents’ capacities is distinct from the substantive question of which considerations actually favour which actions, and positions can combine in more ways than the labels suggest.
depth.secondExample: Consider the wrong kind of reason, and then a case of structural irrationality. A powerful being offers to destroy something you value unless you admire him, and can be counted on to carry out the threat; you therefore have some reason to bring it about that you admire him, yet the threat gives you no reason to think he has any admirable quality. So the reasons for attitudes float free of the reasons about attitudes’ objects. Applications of this distinction are widespread: a large bonus gives a reason to want to want a job, but not a reason to want the job, and a scheme that pays judges for convictions gives reasons about outcomes without giving reasons bearing on guilt. Now consider an agent with perfectly coherent beliefs about the means and ends, who adopts an end and then takes no step toward it, while holding that the step is required for the end. Nothing is wrong with her information and nothing recommends a different end on her own values. She just will not move. She is structurally irrational with respect to her own commitments, and this kind of irrationality needs no claim about which ends are worth having; it is a failure of coherence. That this diagnosis applies even to a case where the agent’s ends are vulgar shows why structural rationality and substantive rationality must be separated, and it exposes an error in arguments that conclude from a person’s inconsistency alone that her aims are bad.
depth.mistake: The standard error is to hear internalism as the doctrine that people have reasons only for whatever they happen to desire, then to refute it with a case in which someone has a reason she does not want to have. That refutes a crude Humean view, not Williams’s. His set includes loyalties, commitments, and evaluative dispositions, and his point is about the route by which considerations can become practical conclusions, not about the absence of concerns that outrank desire. The mirror error is to hear externalism as the doctrine that reasons are mysterious mind-independent facts with no connection to agency at all. Diagnostic procedure: ask what role reasons are supposed to play in your argument, explaining action, advising an agent, or stating a fact that is independent of any agent’s psychology, and see whether the role you assigned is the one your example tests. A further trap is to move from the existence of a wrong-kind-of-reason case to general scepticism about reasons for attitudes, since the puzzle shows only that the reasons-for-attitudes relation needs a restriction, not that it is unintelligible.
depth.application: Non-blocking task. Take four claims and classify each, with a one-sentence justification for the classification: (1) ‘Tomas has a reason to cancel the subscription, though he feels no inclination to do so and nothing in his aims moves him to cancel’; (2) ‘Rosa has a reason to leave the meeting, since her flight departs in ninety minutes and she intends to make it’; (3) ‘These recruits have a reason to cheer for the director’s speech, since he controls their careers, but nothing in the speech deserves praise’; (4) ‘Having promised to review the draft, Mal has a reason to review it, though he has no desire to read it and no project it serves.’ For each, state whether it is internalist or externalist in its implication and whether it is a wrong-kind-of-reason claim. Model response: (1) externalist, since the reason is asserted independently of the set; (2) internalist, since intention plus belief connects by deliberation to the conclusion; (3) wrong kind of reason, an incentive attached to the attitude rather than a feature of the object; (4) contested, and this is where the two positions divide, because internalists must locate the promise among the elements of Mal’s set, treating his commitment itself as the relevant disposition, while externalists cite the force of the promise regardless. Rubric: (1) each classification names the feature that decides it; (2) wrong-kind cases are separated from reasons about the object; (3) the contested case is not falsely resolved; (4) the justification would survive the agent changing her desires, which tests whether the classification was about the reason or about her.
depth.summary: The internalism dispute is about whether the capacity to move an agent is part of what makes a consideration a reason, and the wrong-kind-of-reason problem shows that reasons for attitudes need restrictions that reasons for action may not. Keep three questions apart: which consideration is claimed to favour which attitude, whether the claim depends on the agent’s motivational set, and whether it concerns the object of the attitude or the incentives surrounding it. Those questions transfer directly to the next lesson, where the reasons at issue concern what people deserve and what the state may demand of them.
