visual.title: From a consideration to a conclusion about what to do
visual.description: Show two parallel routes from a consideration to an action, one internal to the agent’s motivational set and one asserted independently of it, and mark where the wrong-kind-of-reason restriction cuts in.
steps: Consideration: the fact or prospect that is said to favour an attitude or action
Motivating route: the consideration figures in the agent’s actual deliberation and explains what she does
Internalist route: sound deliberation from the agent’s motivational set yields the conclusion, so the reason is reachable
Externalist route: the consideration favours the action independently of the set, and the task is to say what makes the claim true
Wrong kind of reason: the incentive attaches to holding the attitude, not to the object of the attitude
Structural rationality: coherence between an agent’s own attitudes, assessed without any claim about which ends are worth having

questions.prompt: A biographer claims her subject is ‘not really the same person’ as the young man who committed an offence, because he disowns that period and will not narrate it as his own. Assess the claim using this level’s distinctions.
questions.answer: The claim runs narrativity as a factual test of identity when it is at most an ideal, so a disavowal that fails the reality constraint leaves the earlier agent answerable rather than replacing him
questions.distractor: The claim is sound, since a person who cannot narrate his past as his own has lost the self to which the criminal law attaches liability
questions.correction: Narrativity comes in two strengths: as a constitutive condition on selfhood and as an ideal of how to live. The subject’s refusal goes to the ideal, and the reality constraint in lesson 81 blocks the inference to a different person, so responsibility for the earlier conduct is not dissolved by an unattractive self-account.

questions.prompt: A researcher announces that her model reproduces every behavioural signature associated with pain, including withdrawal, protective behaviour, and self-report, and concludes that the system feels pain as she does. Evaluate the inference.
questions.answer: She has answered the easy problems and asserted a bridge to the hard problem, since nothing in the functional account establishes that experience accompanies the function
questions.distractor: She has resolved the hard problem, because reproducing every behavioural signature is the only evidence one could have for attributing experience to another system
questions.correction: Reproducing the signatures answers the functional question, which is exactly what Chalmers expects to be tractable. The move from matching behaviour to present experience is the contested step, and it is contested precisely because the conceivability of a functionally identical system without experience is the point at issue.

questions.prompt: A manager reprimands an employee for conduct that the manager engages in publicly every week, and the reprimand’s description of the conduct is accurate. Which condition of a responsibility claim is defective?
questions.answer: Standing, since the warrant for the attitude may be intact while this particular party is not positioned to make the demand
questions.distractor: Attributability, since the employee’s conduct was not after all an expression of his own character
questions.correction: Nothing in the scenario undermines the description of the act or its connection to the employee’s character, so attributability is intact. What fails is the blamer’s position, which lesson 83 treats as a condition on the holder rather than on the agent, and which is why the reprimand misdescribes itself as a demand between equals.

questions.prompt: An agent knowingly and deliberately harms another, and her capacity to recognise and act on reasons is unimpaired at the time. Her ruthlessness was instilled in infancy by a group that raised her to be exactly this way. Which premise does a soft-line reply to the manipulation argument attack?
questions.answer: The parity premise, by arguing that in the manipulated cases the action does not flow from the agent’s own evaluation of reasons in the way it does in the ordinary case
questions.distractor: The conclusion, by showing that the outcome was caused, which compatibilists deny is incompatible with responsibility
questions.correction: Soft-line replies accept the verdict about manipulation cases and locate a difference inside the cases, so they must attack the claim that no responsibility-relevant feature distinguishes them. Denying that causation and responsibility conflict is a general compatibilist move and does not engage this argument, which stipulates reasons-responsiveness in both cases.

questions.prompt: A contractor says of an unusually large completion bonus: ‘the bonus gives me a reason to want to want the signature, but it gives me no reason to think the contract is a good one.’ Which structure is she reporting?
questions.answer: A reason of the wrong kind, since the incentive attaches to holding the attitude rather than to the merits of the object of the attitude
questions.distractor: A motivating reason generated by her motivational set, since the bonus gives her something she already cares about
questions.correction: The wrong-kind-of-reason problem concerns reasons that bear on adopting an attitude rather than on the object the attitude is about. Her care about the money explains why the incentive moves her, which is a fact about motivation, but it does not supply a reason bearing on the contract’s merits, which is the distinction being drawn.

units.title: Desert, testimony, and the limits of legitimate authority

lessons.title: Desert, luck, and equality: does responsibility fix what people are owed?
lessons.explanation: Theories of distributive justice differ over what grounds a claim to a share. Desert-based theories hold that a person may be owed treatment because of a quality or conduct, the desert base, that makes the treatment fitting: pay may be deserved for work, blame for wrongdoing, reward for effort. Luck egalitarianism instead tracks responsibility. Its central claim is that inequalities are acceptable when they express the choices of those who bear them, and unacceptable when they reflect what Derek Parfit and Ronald Dworkin call brute luck, the outcomes that fall on a person independently of any choice. Dworkin’s version, equality of resources, asks what people would agree to if they bargained behind a suitable veil of ignorance, combining an auction that distributes resources according to what people would pay for them with a hypothetical insurance market that prices the risks each person faces. Elizabeth Anderson’s ‘What Is the Point of Equality?’ is the sharpest critical statement. Her first charge is that luck egalitarianism abandons, first, those whose misfortunes stem from their own choices, telling the imprudent driver that his broken leg is his own problem, and second, those who are not productive, consigning the untalented to a status of inferiority. Her second charge is a premise about the structure of choice: that the choiceworthiness of an option does not justify the set of options among which the choice is made, so a worker who takes a hazardous job because nothing else is available has not thereby made the danger her responsibility. Her alternative ideal, democratic equality, aims at equal standing rather than a particular distribution. All of these positions are live and contested, and the debate turns as much on what responsibility can bear as on what equality requires.
lessons.example: Take an illustration, invented for arithmetic and not a quotation from any author. Ali and Bo each begin with 100 units of resources. Bo holds hers. Ali takes a gamble that pays nothing half the time and everything half the time, risking 60 units. Ali’s expected position is 0.5 × 40 + 0.5 × 100 = 70, so the gamble is a fair-ish choice relative to her set of options, and she loses, ending at 40 while Bo stands at 100. A strict luck egalitarian who treats this as option luck draws no obligation to compensate: the shortfall traces to a choice, so 40 and 100 stand. A rule that equalises to the mean would transfer 30 units, leaving Ali and Bo at 70 each, and the total is unchanged at 140. A sufficientarian rule that guarantees no one falls below 60 would transfer 20 units, leaving Ali at 60 and Bo at 80, again totalling 140. Now hold the numbers fixed and change one fact: the loss was not a gamble but a falling rock that no choice could have prevented. Every serious view now agrees Ali should be restored, which means the very same transfer of 30 units can be required by one theory and forbidden by another, depending entirely on whether the loss was chosen. That is the pedagogical point of the illustration: distributions alone do not identify theories, because the same pattern of holdings can be justified in incompatible ways. Anderson’s objection then bites at the second step. If Ali had to choose between the gamble and destitution, so that her option set was itself defective, describing her choice as free does not answer whether the option set was just, and the arithmetic cannot tell us how to describe the choice, because the description is a normative judgment rather than a computation.
lessons.question: What is the core of what the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy calls Rawls’s metaphysical argument against grounding distributive shares in desert?
lessons.answer: That the traits and efforts for which a person might claim desert are themselves products of factors such as family and native endowment that the person did not deserve, so desert cannot bear the weight placed on it
lessons.distractor: That no institution can reliably measure how much effort or contribution each person makes, so desert claims are impractical to apply
lessons.correction: That is the epistemological and pragmatic argument, which is a separate objection that grants desert’s normative relevance and doubts our ability to detect it. Rawls’s metaphysical argument denies that desert can ground shares even in principle, because the desert base is itself undeserved. Distinguishing the two matters, since one is a problem of measurement and the other a problem of warrant, and only the second threatens desert-based theories at their foundation.

depth.definitions: Desert involves a subject, a mode of treatment, and a desert base, the feature in virtue of which the treatment is fitting. Institutional desert is desert under the rules of a practice, as when a competitor deserves the prize for running fastest; pre-institutional desert is not dependent on the rules. Brute luck is what happens to a person independently of her choices; option luck is the outcome of a deliberate gamble. Luck egalitarianism holds that justice requires neutralising brute luck while holding people to their choices. Equality of resources is Dworkin’s construction, using an auction for resources and a hypothetical insurance market for risks. Equality of opportunity for welfare or advantage, associated with Richard Arneson, replaces resources with opportunity sets. Democratic or relational equality is Anderson’s alternative, treating equal social standing rather than any particular distribution as the object of justice. Sufficientarianism guarantees a threshold instead of a relation, and prioritarianism weights benefits to the worse off without demanding equality. The illustration in this lesson deliberately supplies no authority for its numbers; they are a construction for demonstrating the structure of the claims.
depth.mechanism: Luck egalitarianism is derived in two steps. The first is a claim about the point of equality: since inequalities that reflect no one’s choice treat like cases differently for reasons irrelevant to responsibility, equality requires removing them. The second is an operational claim about what counts as a choice, which is where the theory becomes vulnerable. Dworkin’s device is a hypothetical insurance market in which people price risks before knowing whether they will face them, so that the level of provision for disability or unemployment is fixed by what a rational insurer would have bought rather than by sympathy or political clout; this gives responsibility-tracking a procedural answer instead of relying on moralising about who deserved what. Every step attracts attack. Identifying which losses were chosen is epistemically difficult, and judgments about it track social position, which is why Anderson warns against distributing blame along with benefits. The abandonment objection holds that a theory which leaves the imprudent driver unaided treats her as outside the community of equals, and this objection does not depend on whether the theory’s responsibility judgments are accurate. The regress objection from lesson 84 attacks from the other side: if an agent’s capacity to make the choice she made is itself the product of unchosen conditions, responsibility for outcomes becomes hard to locate, and a responsibility-tracking theory may find itself unable to track anything. The option-set objection attacks the premise that choice can be assessed without first assessing the alternatives, which is precisely the judgment the theory wanted to avoid. Relational equality avoids the abandonment problem and faces its own: if standing is what matters, comparatively large material inequalities might be acceptable provided the relationships are respectful, a prospect many egalitarians reject. The controversy is unresolved and the readings present it as such.
depth.secondExample: Apply the same structure to a case in the news cycle’s favourite example, student debt, and to one where desert and responsibility point in opposite directions. A graduate borrowed to fund a degree that did not improve her earnings. Responsibility-sensitive reasoning asks whether the borrowing was a defensible choice given her information and alternatives at the time, and compensation tracks the answer: if she chose with adequate information and reasonable options, the loss is hers; if she was sold a false prospectus with no realistic alternative, it is not. Desert-based reasoning asks a different question, namely whether her effort and contribution warrant a subsidy, which can favour relief for a diligent graduate in an unproductive occupation and withhold it from an idle one who chose wisely. Notice that the two criteria can yield opposite verdicts in the same case, which is why a policy argument that switches between them without saying so can appear inconsistent while each individual step is defensible. A second application sharpens the point about option sets. Compare two workers in hazardous jobs. The first has cheap alternatives and takes the wage premium; the second can find no work at all otherwise. On a choice-based criterion both look like they have chosen the hazard, yet a relational egalitarian holds that the second has been denied equal standing in the labour market, and that the remedy is a change in the option set, such as enforcement and mobility, rather than a payment calibrated to her degree of fault. Same risk, two different remedies, because the theories disagree about what the injustice is.
depth.mistake: The signature mistake is to treat equality as sameness of holdings and then to argue that a departure from sameness is unfair whatever its cause, which ignores the responsibility axis entirely; the companion mistake is the reverse, assuming that because an inequality traces to a choice it is therefore just, which Anderson explicitly denies. A third and subtler error is to assume that a policy’s justification is irrelevant once its effects are correct. On the contrary, the justification often determines how the recipients are treated, which is why two schemes with identical transfer amounts can differ in whether they express respect or the assignment of blame for being needy. Diagnostics: for any distributive claim, ask which criterion is being used, consent, contribution, effort, compensation for unchosen loss, or equal standing; check that a single criterion governs the whole argument; and check whether the argument has quietly switched criteria partway through.
depth.application: Non-blocking task. Choose one policy proposal with a plausible individual-responsibility component, such as means-tested debt relief, compensation after a flood, or hazard pay in an essential industry. Write four sections. (1) State the rule precisely enough that it can be applied to the illustration used in this lesson, and compute the transfers for the Ali and Bo cases under your rule, showing that the total is unchanged. (2) Name the criterion grounding the rule, from the list above. (3) State one case in which your rule produces a result you find unjust and explain whether the fault lies in the criterion or in the case. (4) State which objection from Anderson or from the regress argument most threatens your view. Model response for means-tested flood compensation: (1) compensate losses above a stated fraction of assets, so Ali at 40 and Bo at 100 receive equal compensation per unit of loss if both lost the same assets, and the post-transfer total equals the pre-transfer total by construction; (2) the criterion is compensation for unchosen loss, with the threshold as a rough proxy for avoidable exposure; (3) a household that could have insured but was misled by a broker exposes that the proxy cannot separate choice from information, which is a defect in the operational rule rather than in the criterion of unchosen loss; (4) the option-set objection applies because some affected households had no insurable alternative. Rubric: (1) the arithmetic is shown and conserved; (2) exactly one criterion is named, with any secondary criterion flagged; (3) the counter-case is a genuine case for your own rule; (4) the objection is identified by name and its mechanism stated.
depth.summary: Desert and responsibility are distinct grounds for distribution, and both must answer to the objection that the traits and choices they cite may themselves be unchosen, which is the regress of lesson 84 arriving in political philosophy. Keep the three questions separate in every distributive argument: what treatment is claimed, in virtue of what feature, and whether that feature can survive the regress. This is the analytical skill that a debate about equality, merit, and luck actually requires, and it is the same structure you will use when the contested question concerns whose testimony counts as credible.

lessons.title: Epistemic injustice: credibility, interpretation, and whose testimony counts
lessons.explanation: The level so far has treated testimony as a source of knowledge and testimony’s hearers as rational agents weighing evidence. Miranda Fricker’s work adds a dimension that pure epistemology tends to miss: the hearer’s credibility judgment can be distorted by prejudice, and the resulting harm is both epistemic and moral. She distinguishes two kinds. Testimonial injustice occurs when a speaker receives a credibility deficit because of an identity prejudice in the hearer: she is believed less than her evidence warrants, and the deficit is not a correction of her reliability but a transmission of social prejudice. Hermeneutical injustice occurs when a speaker is unfairly disadvantaged in making sense of her own social experience because the collective interpretive resources available to her are inadequate, and the inadequacy tracks her social position. Fricker’s remedy for the first is a virtue: testimonial justice, the trained disposition to correct for prejudice in one’s credibility judgments. Later authors broaden the diagnosis. Kristie Dotson describes testimonial smothering, in which a speaker withholds testimony she knows will not be received, and contributory injustice, in which a hearer’s own interpretive practices deprive a speaker of the resources she would need to be understood at all. José Medina argues that resistance and collective change, not individual virtue alone, are required. Charles Mills’s epistemologies of ignorance analyse the active production of not-knowing as a feature of a social order rather than a mere gap. Whether the concept of epistemic injustice has grown too elastic to do analytical work is contested, and this lesson keeps that objection visible.
lessons.example: A city water authority receives repeated reports from one neighbourhood that the tap water smells wrong and that residents have been unwell. Intake staff treat the reports as exaggerated, partly because the callers are described in the system as frequent complainers and partly because the callers’ accent and address are associated, in the staff’s unexamined expectations, with unreliable reports. The complaints are recorded at low priority. Months later, sampling confirms contamination. Reconstruct the failure by kind. Testimonial injustice is the credibility deficit itself: the reports were discounted at least partly because of a prejudice keyed to identity rather than because of any evidence about these particular reports, and the mechanism is visible in the fact that identical reports from another neighbourhood were escalated. Hermeneutical injustice is a second and different failure: the residents could describe the smell but had no available vocabulary or institutional category for long-term low-level contamination, and the authority’s intake form offered only the options ‘taste and odour complaint’ and ‘possible leak’, neither of which mapped to what they were reporting, so their experience was not merely disbelieved but unsayable in the terms the institution could process. Contributory injustice names the third layer: the institution’s own interpretive practices actively consumed the resources that would have let it hear the report, so the deficiency is not a gap in the residents’ understanding but a consequence of whose categories counted. Now add the contrast case that keeps the concept honest. Suppose a different set of calls came from a known group of fraudsters running a compensation scheme. Discounting those reports is not testimonial injustice; it is warranted credibility assessment, and a theory that could not distinguish the cases would be useless. The distinguishing feature is that the deficit in the first case is not a function of the evidence about the speaker’s reliability in this matter.
lessons.question: Which formulation captures the difference between testimonial injustice and hermeneutical injustice as Fricker draws it?
lessons.answer: Testimonial injustice is a hearer’s prejudiced credibility judgment, while hermeneutical injustice is a shortfall in shared interpretive resources that disadvantages a speaker in understanding her own experience
lessons.distractor: Testimonial injustice concerns the hearer’s mistaken beliefs about a speaker, while hermeneutical injustice concerns the speaker’s own ignorance about the subject at issue
lessons.correction: The second half locates hermeneutical injustice in the speaker’s deficiency, which reverses Fricker’s point. She locates it in the collective resources, which are shaped by whose experience has been worth recording. A speaker can be fully informed about her life and still unable to render it intelligible in the categories available to her audience, and that is the wrong she identifies.

depth.definitions: Epistemic injustice is a wrong done to someone in her capacity as a knower or a participant in interpretive practices. Testimonial injustice is a credibility deficit or excess produced by identity prejudice rather than by evidence about the speaker’s competence. The credibility economy is the distribution of belief and uptake among participants. Identity prejudice is a prejudice tracking a social identity rather than the individual’s conduct. Hermeneutical injustice is an unfair disadvantage in making sense of one’s own experience, caused by the under-development of collective interpretive resources attributable to a group’s marginalisation. Testimonial smothering is Dotson’s term for a speaker’s self-silencing in the face of predictable non-uptake. Contributory injustice occurs when a hearer’s interpretive practices block a speaker’s sense-making rather than merely failing to help it. Epistemologies of ignorance, in Mills’s usage, treat not-knowing as produced and maintained rather than as an absence. Standing to hold responsible, from lesson 83, is a close structural analogue: in both cases the question is not only whether a claim is true but whether this person may make it.
depth.mechanism: Credibility judgments have a dual aspect, and the mechanism of the wrong lies in that duality. Judging that a speaker is likely to be right is an evidential judgment, revised by track record, corroboration, and plausibility; but it is also a social act that assigns or withholds recognition, and it is performed under cognitive pressures that favour quick heuristics about who is likely to be reliable. Those heuristics track genuine statistical patterns often enough to be useful and unjust often enough to be dangerous, and the danger is greatest where the pattern is a stereotype about a social group rather than a fact about the individual. Structural considerations extend the analysis beyond individual vice. Documentation practices determine who can register a claim; category systems determine what can be claimed; gatekeeping determines whose framing of a situation enters the record; and administrative incentives determine which reports are worth pursuing. The remedies therefore come in incompatible flavours. Fricker’s virtue approach trains hearers to correct their judgments and preserves the ordinary practice of credibility assessment. Structural approaches change who sits on the body that judges, in the belief that individual virtue cannot survive an incentive structure that rewards dismissal. Skeptical critics press two objections. The first is that the concept risks moralising ordinary evidential judgment, so that any discounting of a group’s reports is treated as injustice even when base rates in a specific domain would warrant caution; the reply distinguishes prejudice from evidence-sensitive generalisation but must show how to tell them apart in practice. The second is that an elastic notion of injustice becomes an accusation rather than an analysis, which is why the literature now works hard on demarcation criteria. Neither objection is settled.
depth.secondExample: Consider a laboratory dispute, and then a case where the remedy makes things worse. A technician reports that a sample was mishandled. In the first variant the supervisor discounts the report because she has formed the settled expectation that people of the technician’s age and background are careless; this is a credibility deficit whose cause is not evidence about this technician’s record, and a hearing that corrected for the prejudice would have followed up immediately. In the second variant the supervisor discounts the report because the technician’s log shows the sample was never refrigerated; the discount is warranted, and the technology of virtue is irrelevant because the judgment is already tracking evidence. The two variants are formally identical from the outside, which is why the analysis must reach the basis of the judgment rather than the outcome. Now the third variant. Suppose the technician, after several years of having her reports quietly dropped, stops reporting minor problems altogether, expecting nothing. Dotson’s smothering explains the omission without attributing any new fault to the hearer at the moment of the failure: the silencing was produced earlier, and the practice is now self-confirming, since a technician who reports nothing appears to have nothing to report. Finally, consider a remedy that backfires. A committee introduces a rule that any complaint from a designated group must be escalated, regardless of its content. The rule reduces the specific deficit Fricker identified and creates two new problems: reports that are unmeritorious can no longer be dismissed on their merits, which degrades the institution’s epistemic performance, and the rule makes the group’s credibility depend on a mandate rather than on the force of what is said, which many of the very speakers it aims to protect find demeaning. Remedies have epistemic costs and they should be stated and weighed rather than assumed to be free.
depth.mistake: Two reductions dominate. The first equates epistemic injustice with rudeness, incivility, or being contradicted, which loses the concept’s content: what makes the wrong distinctive is that a prejudiced judgment about credibility or interpretive capacity damages someone as a knower. The second, and more philosophically serious, assumes the analysis requires an individual villain with an ascertainable prejudice. It does not, as the smothering and contributory cases show, and the assumption makes structural harms invisible in exactly the way the theory was designed to prevent. Diagnostic questions: what is the judgment that wrongs the speaker, and is it a credibility judgment or an interpretive one? What is the evidence that the judgment was driven by identity rather than by facts about this speaker? And what would have happened to an identically situated speaker with a different identity? Only a case that can answer the third question has done the work needed to call anything an injustice.
depth.application: Non-blocking task. Select an institutional intake process, for instance a workplace grievance procedure, a public comment period on a planning decision, or a service complaint line. Audit it for the two forms of injustice and write a short report with four parts. (1) Identify one point where a credibility judgment is made and state the basis on which it is made in the ordinary case. (2) Identify one point where the available categories or forms constrain what a complainant can express. (3) Propose one remedy for each and state its epistemic cost. (4) State one objection a sceptical critic would raise about your second finding and answer it. Model response for a planning comment period: (1) the case officer weighs comments by whether the commenter is described as a ‘stakeholder’, a category assigned by postcode, so the credibility proxy tracks residence rather than knowledge of the site; (2) the online form permits support, opposition, or an objection on one of four listed grounds, so concerns about cumulative effects across several developments cannot be entered at all, a hermeneutical limit that is not attributable to any officer’s prejudice; (3) a remedy for (1) is to record the substance of each comment with a stated reason for weight, whose epistemic cost is more case-officer time; a remedy for (2) is an open-text ground requiring a written rationale, whose cost is a larger volume of less tractable material; (4) the sceptical critic will say that residence is a legitimate proxy for interest and that the form must prioritise triage, and the reply distinguishes interest from expertise, which addresses the objection only partly. Rubric: (1) the credibility judgment is located in a specific procedural step; (2) the interpretive constraint is not the same finding restated; (3) each remedy has a stated cost rather than being obviously correct; (4) the objection is a real one and the answer concedes what it must.
depth.summary: Epistemic injustice explains how prejudice can corrupt credibility and how structural arrangements can make experience unsayable, and it forces epistemology to account for who is believed rather than only for what is true. Keep three questions in hand: whose credibility judgment is at issue, whether the basis of that judgment would survive a change in the speaker’s identity, and whether the failure lies in a person or in the interpretive resources and procedures. Those questions reappear when the knower is not a person at all but a procedure, which is the problem the final lessons take up.

lessons.title: Legitimacy and the limits of authority: neutrality, judicial review, and where the state stops
lessons.explanation: Lesson 61 separated authority from getting things right; this lesson asks where legitimate authority ends. Two distinctions do the work. The first is between legitimacy and justice. A rule can be legitimate, in the sense that its imposition does not wrong those subject to it, while also being unjust; Rawls uses this gap to explain why citizens who disagree with a law may still be bound to comply with it within limits, so long as the power is exercised in accordance with a constitution whose essentials all may reasonably be expected to endorse. Collapsing the two either licenses obedience to anything enacted or makes every unjust law a licence for resistance, and both results are worse than the distinction. The second is between legitimacy and obligation, which lesson 78 separated: legitimacy is a property of the exercise of power, obligation is a bond on a particular person, and philosophical anarchists accept the first while denying the second. With the distinctions in place, the question of limits becomes tractable. Joseph Raz’s service conception holds that a directive has practical authority over you when following it leaves you better able to act on the reasons that already apply to you than deciding for yourself, which also gives the scope of the authority: it extends only as far as the justification does. That raises the disputed boundary questions of this lesson. May the state promote a conception of the good life, or must it remain neutral among them? Who decides whether a law violates a right, a court or a legislature? And what may be done in an emergency, when the ordinary justifications for restraint are strained?
lessons.example: Work three cases through Raz’s criteria, adding the disputed boundary question to each. First, a requirement that practising engineers complete continuing education to retain a licence. The dependent reason is the interest of the public in competent engineering; the directive requires the engineers to treat that reason as settled by the rule rather than re-deciding whether to update their knowledge; the normal justification is that each engineer is more likely to satisfy the reasons that apply to her by following the scheme than by judging case by case when she needs training. The scope condition is instructive: the authority covers the curriculum and the hours, and nobody thinks it extends to the engineer’s choice of employer, because the justification does not reach there. Second, a restriction on a harmless religious or cultural practice whose only basis is that the majority finds the practice distasteful. Here the dependent reasons, which include the interest of each person in living according to her own convictions, do not support the restriction, so a state that imposes it is not serving the reasons that apply to the subjects, and the authority claim fails on its own terms; this is the neutrality question in concrete form, since the state is preferring one conception of the good without being able to show that its subjects fare better by conforming. Third, a statute restricting the time and place of protest in the name of public order. Suppose everyone agrees that some restriction is permissible and that this one is too broad. Who decides? On Waldron’s argument against strong judicial review, in a society with a commitment to rights, functioning democratic institutions, and persistent disagreement about what rights require, there is no reason to expect judges to be more reliable than legislators on rights questions, and depriving citizens of a voice on those questions has its own costs; on the opposing view, legislatures are precisely the bodies whose self-interest and electoral pressure make rights the wrong thing to leave to them, and judicial review gives a second look. Notice that both positions accept that rights matter; the disagreement is about institutional design under disagreement, not about whether rights exist.
lessons.question: According to Raz’s service conception, what makes a state directive a legitimate authority over a particular person?
lessons.answer: That following the directive leaves her better placed to act on the reasons that already apply to her than deciding the matter for herself would
lessons.distractor: That she has undertaken or accepted an obligation to comply with the directives of the institution that issued it
lessons.correction: That is the consent theory, which Raz’s account does not require and which the particularity problem from lesson 78 makes hard to sustain empirically. The service conception grounds authority in the improvement that deference makes to the subject’s own conformity with reason, not in any act of acceptance, and that is why the same account generates a scope limit, since deference is justified only where it helps.

depth.definitions: Legitimacy is the property of an exercise of political power such that its imposition does not wrong those subject to it; justice concerns whether the content of a rule or decision is right. Practical authority is a right to direct and a corresponding duty of deference in the addressee. On Raz’s account, the dependence thesis holds that authoritative directives should be based on reasons that already apply to the subjects independently of the directive, the preemption thesis holds that a directive replaces those first-order reasons rather than adding to them, and the normal justification thesis supplies the standing reason to treat the directive as authoritative. Neutrality is the requirement that the state not justify its actions by appeal to any particular conception of the good life; perfectionism denies that requirement and permits promotion of valuable ways of living. Judicial review is the power of courts to invalidate legislation for inconsistency with a constitution or rights instrument. Derogation is the suspension of ordinary protections in an emergency, with the legal question being who determines that an emergency exists and what survives the suspension. The demos problem is the question of who constitutes the political body whose decisions claim authority. Prerequisites: the distinction between legitimacy and obligation from lessons 61 and 78, and public reason from lesson 63.
depth.mechanism: The puzzle of political authority is that it seems to require a person to act on another’s judgment rather than her own, which is why consent theories are attractive: only an act of the subject’s own will seems to remove the offence. Consent theories then fail on the facts, since most people have not consented and their non-consent is not treated as decisive, and on the merits, since the content of one’s obligation would then depend on the breadth of an agreement nobody remembers making. The service conception offers a different solution: authority is justified instrumentally, by the improvement in the subject’s conformity with reasons, which means the justification and the limit are the same argument considered from two directions. From that structure follow the standard boundary disputes. The neutrality debate turns on whether the improvement in question can include the subject’s living a more valuable life, which perfectionists affirm and their opponents deny on the ground that the state is a poor judge of value and that its judgments fall unevenly on minorities. The judicial review debate turns on comparative institutional reliability under disagreement: an epistemic division of labour, not a disagreement about rights. The emergency debate turns on whether the preemption thesis can justify directives whose content is not available for scrutiny, and on the danger that a power to suspend the ordinary framework becomes a power to redefine it. Each dispute has a characteristic failure mode. A state that treats every disagreement as bad faith loses the epistemic benefits of contestation; a state that leaves rights entirely to majorities is exposed to the risk those rights exist to prevent; and a state that concentrates the definition of emergency in the executive tends to keep the emergency. Raz himself allows that authority can be piecemeal rather than all-or-nothing, which means the question is rarely whether a state is legitimate but which domains and decisions are.
depth.secondExample: Test the boundaries on a live question: a state requires all residents to hold a digital identity credential, linked to tax, benefits, and banking, to access public services. Analyse it under three headings. Under the dependence thesis, the reasons that already apply to residents include accessing benefits and paying taxes, and the scheme plausibly improves their ability to do so, which supports authority in the domain of service delivery. Under the limits of that justification, the same reasons do not support requiring the credential for assembling, speaking, or using transport, so the scope of the authority is narrower than the scope of the requirement as drafted, and a defender must either narrow the requirement or supply separate reasons for the further uses. Under neutrality, the question is whether the scheme entrenches a preferred way of life by making continuous administrative visibility a condition of ordinary participation, which is a substantive objection rather than a technical one. Under the institutional question, suppose the enabling statute is challenged for disproportionate interference with privacy and association; the relevant dispute is uncommonly well suited to a legislature, since it involves trade-offs in public administration, which is a point in Waldron’s favour, and uncommonly dangerous to leave there, since the affected group is a minority of unpopular users and the harms are diffuse, which is the point in favour of review. Answering the case requires taking a position on institutional reliability, not merely on rights, which is what an honest verdict must record.
depth.mistake: Two confusions recur. The first treats a legitimate decision as one that is merely lawful or effective, which removes the moral content of the concept: issuing a rule through the correct procedure does not settle whether imposing it wrongs anyone. The second treats the discovery that authority has limits as a permission to disregard anything one happens to oppose, which ignores the distinction between a law being unjust and its being illegitimate, and ignores the obligation question entirely. Diagnostics: for a legitimacy claim, state the dependent reasons, ask whose conformity with them improves and how much, and then ask whether the directive’s scope matches the justification, because scope overreach is the most common defect in real cases and the least often named. For a disagreement over the right institutional decision-maker, ask what comparative reliability claim is being made, since a theory that simply prefers judges or legislatures has not yet offered one.
depth.application: Non-blocking task. Choose a policy that imposes a requirement on everyone in a domain, for instance mandatory participation in an administrative scheme, a licensing requirement for an occupation, or a restriction on a form of assembly. Write a legitimacy assessment with five parts. (1) The dependent reasons that apply to the subjects independently of the policy. (2) The improvement claimed and the evidence that would support it. (3) The scope of the authority your justification supports, stated deliberately narrower or wider than the policy as drafted. (4) The neutrality question: whether the justification appeals to a conception of the good life, and why that does or does not disqualify it. (5) The institutional question: which body should decide contested cases under your view, with a comparative reliability claim. Model response for an occupational licensing requirement: (1) the dependent reasons are the interests of clients and third parties in competence and the practitioner’s interest in a career; (2) the improvement is fewer competence failures, and the evidence needed is comparative failure rates under licensed and unlicensed practice, which is often unavailable, an honest finding; (3) the scope supported is competence assurance, not the promotion of a particular professional culture, so rules about dress or association would exceed it; (4) the justification is neutral, since competence is a reason for everyone; (5) contested cases should first go to a technical body with limited jurisdiction, because it has relevant expertise, with an appeal to a general court for grounds beyond competence, a division that concedes something to both sides. Rubric: (1) dependent reasons are stated as reasons, not as facts; (2) the improvement claim names what evidence would vindicate it; (3) the scope section is narrower or wider than the policy and says so; (4) the neutrality discussion does not merely assert neutrality; (5) the institutional claim is comparative.
depth.summary: Legitimacy is a property of imposed power, not of the correctness of what is imposed, and the service conception makes the justification of authority and its limit one argument. The transferable skill is to state the reasons that already apply to the subjects, ask whether deference improves their conformity with those reasons, and then check whether the directive’s scope matches. That same structure is what the final pair of lessons applies to a case where the issuing authority is not a person and the reasons are not wholly transparent.

lessons.title: Working a genuinely unsettled question: higher-order evidence, defeaters, and reflective equilibrium
lessons.explanation: Lessons 79 and 80 taught the construction and evaluation of arguments. This lesson adds the situation where the arguments have been built and evaluated and the question is still open. Two things make that situation hard. The first is higher-order evidence, which is evidence about the epistemic status of your own reasoning and your own evidence: the fact that a competent person reached the opposite conclusion, that you reasoned while tired, that your informants are all downstream of one source. The second is that the debate may be genuinely unsettled, so that a verdict is not available and the honest output is a position with a stated confidence level and a statement of what would change it. On peer disagreement, four views dominate and none is settled. The equal weight view, defended by Adam Elga and David Christensen, holds that when a peer holding the same evidence disagrees, you should move toward her position by roughly halving the difference. The steadfast view, defended by Thomas Kelly, holds that you may retain your view, since the first-order evidence is your evidence and the disagreement does not by itself diminish it. A justificationist view denies that disagreement affects the justification of a belief that was independently well supported, so no revision is required. The total evidence view holds that the disagreement is simply one more item to weigh with the rest, so its effect depends on what the rest supports. Alongside these sits the method of reflective equilibrium, introduced by John Rawls: move back and forth between considered judgements about cases and general principles, adjusting each until a coherent set is reached, and prefer a wide equilibrium in which alternative principles have been tested against the same judgements.
lessons.example: You hold, after the previous lesson, that a state may require a digital credential for access to services but not for political activity. A colleague you regard as an epistemic peer, with the same information and a comparable record on these questions, holds that any requirement at all entrenches administrative visibility and should be abandoned. Work the four responses on this one case. On the equal weight view, your credence in your own position should move substantially toward hers, not because she has evidence you lack but because the disagreement itself is evidence that your reasoning is as likely as hers to have gone wrong. On the steadfast view, nothing has changed: you have already weighed the objection that she is making, and repeating it more confidently does not add to your evidence. On the total evidence view, ask what your initial evidence supported and how much weight the fact of disagreement carries: if your case rests on a general institutional argument and hers on a specific objection you have already answered, the disagreement lowers your confidence by less than the equal weight view implies. Then apply reflective equilibrium in a way that can actually be audited. Write down the principle you are using, which is something like ‘state requirements are permissible when they improve conformity with reasons that already apply to the subjects, and impermissible when their justification depends on a contested conception of the good’. Test it against a case you are confident about: a requirement that benefits be claimed through an online system. Test it against a case you find uncomfortable: a requirement that identification be presented at a polling station, which many regard as an ordinary administrative measure and others as a barrier. If your principle cannot sort these cases, you adjust the principle, not the case. What you may not do is adjust the case to save the principle, which is the failure mode that makes equilibrium a system for laundering prior commitments.
lessons.question: Which statement best distinguishes the equal weight view from the total evidence view of peer disagreement?
lessons.answer: The equal weight view treats a peer’s disagreement as a reason to split the difference in confidence, whereas the total evidence view treats it as one more item of evidence whose weight depends on what the rest of the evidence supports
lessons.distractor: The equal weight view requires suspending judgement, whereas the total evidence view requires retaining your original view whenever your reasoning was sound
lessons.correction: The second clause describes the steadfast or justificationist position, not the total evidence view, and the first clause overstates equal weight, which requires moving toward the peer rather than full suspension. The real contrast is about whether disagreement enters as a discrete, roughly mechanical weight or as an item whose significance varies with the rest of the evidence.

depth.definitions: Higher-order evidence bears on the reliability of your reasoning rather than on the subject matter. An epistemic peer is someone with the same evidence and comparable competence on the question; a superior, inferior, or interested party is not a peer, which is why the puzzle is narrower than ordinary disagreement. A rebutting defeater is evidence that your belief is false; an undercutting defeater is evidence that the grounds of your belief are unreliable, leaving the truth of the matter unaddressed. Conciliationism is the family of views requiring belief revision in the face of disagreement; steadfastness denies it; the justificationist view holds that justification is determined by the evidence available to the agent and is unaffected by disagreement. A considered judgement, in Rawls’s method, is a judgement made under conditions favourable to accuracy, and reflective equilibrium is the coherence between such judgements and principles. Narrow equilibrium settles one question; wide equilibrium tests a whole scheme of principles against a broad set of judgements. Underdetermination is the situation in which the available evidence supports more than one hypothesis, which is a distinct problem from disagreement and often accompanies it.
depth.mechanism: Higher-order evidence creates a two-level structure, and nearly all the interest in this area comes from the friction between the levels. At the object level, the evidence may strongly support a conclusion. At the higher level, the fact that your reasoning produced a disputed result is itself information about your reasoning. If you treat the higher level as decisive you risk scepticism, since every disputed view has a disputant; if you ignore it you risk dogmatism, since you will never be moved by the discovery that your procedure is unreliable in this domain. Several resources reduce the friction without collapsing either level. First, the peer condition: most disagreement is not peer disagreement, and establishing parity requires evidence about the other party’s evidence and competence rather than an assumption of symmetry. Second, the identification of error: if you can locate the step at which the two reasoners diverge and evaluate it, you are back in the first-order business of evaluating arguments, which is what lessons 79 and 80 were for. Third, the asymmetry of track records in the specific domain, which is a reason to weight one party’s view more heavily without denying the other’s competence. Reflective equilibrium then supplies a method for output where a verdict is not available, but it has a documented failure mode: the judgements that anchor it are not neutral, and critics in the tradition of lesson 87 argue that a method which takes considered judgements as data will systematise the intuitions of whichever social position produced them, since people who were never exposed to an injustice will not register it as an intuition. The reply is not that equilibrium is worthless but that its inputs need auditing, and that a reader should be able to trace which judgement an adjustment served.
depth.secondExample: Consider a case where the disagreement is real but the parties are not peers, and then a case where an undercutting defeater arrives without any disagreement. In the first case, two engineers disagree about whether a design is safe. One has reviewed the failure data and the relevant code; the other holds the same professional credentials and has read the summary. The credentials are equal, the evidence is not, and the correct response is to identify the asymmetry rather than to halve the difference; the equal weight view does not apply, and applying it produces a manufactured symmetry in which a summary and a dataset count as the same thing. In the second case, a manager discovers that the report she relied on was produced by a process that systematically excluded the slowest cases, and nothing about the substantive issue has changed, no one has disagreed, and the report may be accurate. This is an undercutting defeater, and its correct effect is to lower her confidence until she can estimate the exclusion’s effect, which is a different operation from weighing a counter-argument. The two cases together show the diagnostic sequence this lesson teaches: first check whether the disagreement is among peers, then check whether the defeat is rebutting or undercutting, and only then apply a view about conciliation. Readers who begin with the view about conciliation tend to produce either false equivalence or complacent steadfastness.
depth.mistake: The most common error is to convert every disagreement into evidence of parity, then announce that the question is unresolvable because reasonable people differ. Parity requires argument, and a disagreement between an expert with data and an advocate with an interest is not evidence that the credences should converge. The opposite error is to invoke steadfastness as a licence: retaining a view after an undercutting defeater has reduced your grounds is not steadfastness but obstinacy, and the test is whether you can state what would change your mind and whether you have updated when it appeared. A third error is to mistake reflective equilibrium for coherence alone, ignoring that a tidy set of principles can be tidy precisely because the judgements that would disturb it were never entered; diagnostics: name an input judgement that your scheme makes hard to accommodate, and see whether you adjusted anything in response.
depth.application: Non-blocking task, and the method used in the next lesson. Produce a position dossier of one page for a contested question of your choice, containing seven labelled sections. (1) The question, in one sentence, with the decision it bears on. (2) Two or more positions, each with a named proponent or a named literature, not invented authorities. (3) Your verdict. (4) Your confidence, as a stated level rather than a number you cannot defend. (5) One rebutting defeater for your verdict. (6) One undercutting defeater against the quality of your reasoning. (7) What evidence would change your mind. Then add a final section, (8) the reflective-equilibrium check: one judgement that sits awkwardly with your principle, and a statement of whether you adjusted the principle or left the friction unresolved. Model response for the question whether mandatory voting should be adopted: (1) whether a state may require citizens to vote, bearing on the design of elections; (2) in favour, arguments from the epistemic and equality-based defence of participation discussed in lesson 65; against, arguments from liberty and from the right not to participate in a process one judges corrupt; (3) verdict, permissible only with a no-penalty option, on grounds that the requirement improves conformity with reasons citizens already have; (4) moderate, because the empirical claim about turnout effects is contested; (5) rebutting defeater, evidence that mandated turnout does not improve the informational quality of outcomes, which removes the main justification; (6) undercutting defeater, my reading of the empirical literature is drawn from summary sources; (7) I would change my view if a defensible study showed that coercion reduced participation by the politically alienated; (8) awkward judgement, that a citizen who abstains to protest an unjust system is doing something reasonable, which my principle handles only by granting the exemption that then weakens the mandate, so the friction is left standing rather than resolved by adjusting the case. Rubric: (1) positions are attributed; (2) the two defeaters are of different types and are genuinely about the verdict and the reasoning respectively; (3) the confidence level is tied to a stated reason; (4) the equilibrium section records an unresolved friction rather than ending with a tidy synthesis.
depth.summary: Where the evidence does not settle a question, the deliverable is not a verdict but a position with its defeaters and its exit conditions stated, and the quality of the reasoning is judged by whether the writer can be moved. Keep the diagnostic sequence in order: is the disagreement peer disagreement, is the defeater rebutting or undercutting, and does the equilibrium survive the entry of an uncomfortable judgement. This is the method the capstone applies to a question that is both practically urgent and theoretically unresolved.
