lessons.title: Capstone: opaque risk prediction and the limits of state authority
lessons.explanation: This lesson applies the level’s tools to a question that is live in practice and unresolved in theory: may a state base consequential decisions on statistical risk predictions whose reasoning it cannot explain to the people affected? The decisions in question include setting bail, allocating enforcement attention, prioritising inspections, and granting or withdrawing benefits. Four positions are defensible and none commands consensus. The refusal position holds that opaque predictions are categorically unsuitable for exercises of state power that impose serious burdens, because the subject cannot contest the grounds on which she is treated. The contestability position permits the predictions provided affected individuals receive a reasoned decision, an explanation of the factors that mattered in their case, and a route to challenge the individual outcome. The trade-off position treats the choice among error distributions as the real decision and asks the state to make that choice publicly rather than pretending a model is neutral; this is where the mathematical result of Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan matters, since it shows that when the groups being scored have different base rates, calibration and equal error rates cannot generally be achieved together. The transparency-first position requires interpretable models even at a cost in predictive performance. To assess any of these, the level supplies four instruments: the legitimacy scope test from lesson 88, the credibility and interpretive analysis of lesson 87, the responsibility and desert distinctions of lesson 86, and the disagreement method of lesson 89. The honest verdict will identify what is settled, such as the trade-off result, and what is not, such as whether contestability restores legitimacy.
lessons.example: Take the arithmetic first, because it constrains everything else. Suppose two groups are being scored for a genuinely predictive and genuinely useful outcome, and suppose the predictor ranks individuals perfectly, so every person who will experience the adverse outcome is ranked above every person who will not. Group A has 100 members, 20 of whom will experience the outcome; group B has 100 members, 40 of whom will. A policy selects the top 30 in each group, which satisfies a balance requirement that the same proportion of each group be flagged. In group A, all 20 true positives are selected and 10 people who will not experience the outcome are also selected, so the false positive rate is 10 divided by 80, which is 12.5 per cent, and the false negative rate is zero. In group B, 30 of the 40 true positives are selected, so the false positive rate is zero and the false negative rate is 10 divided by 40, which is 25 per cent. Error rates differ by group even though the predictor is perfectly accurate and the selection rates are identical. The difference is produced by the base rates, and the general lesson, stated for the two-group case by Kleinberg, Mullainathan and Raghavan, is that calibration, balance for the positive class, and balance for the negative class cannot all hold at once unless the prediction is trivial or the base rates coincide. Two consequences follow for policy. First, a claim that a scoring instrument is fair is incomplete until it says which criterion it satisfies and which it sacrifices. Second, a demand that a model satisfy every fairness criterion simultaneously is not a demand that can be met, so a critic who makes it cannot be answered and should instead be asked which error she is willing to accept. The arithmetic does not tell you which criterion to choose; it tells you that the choice is forced and must be justified by the legitimacy argument rather than by the mathematics.
lessons.question: Two groups differ in the base rate of the outcome that a state scoring instrument predicts. What does the trade-off result show about a policy that requires both group-wise calibration and equal false positive rates?
lessons.answer: That the two requirements cannot generally be met at the same time when base rates differ, so the policy must choose which to prioritise and justify that choice
lessons.distractor: That the instrument is biased against one group and should be withdrawn, since a fair instrument would satisfy both requirements
lessons.correction: The result is a structural constraint on any predictor, not a defect in this one, and it holds even for a predictor that ranks perfectly. Bias is a separate question about what the instrument tracks and whether that is a legitimate basis for the decision. Withdrawing the instrument may be the right conclusion, but the trade-off alone does not establish it, and treating the arithmetic as proof of bias leaves you unable to answer the harder question of which error distribution the state should prefer.

depth.definitions: A risk score is a statistical estimate of the probability of an outcome used to inform a decision. Opacity is the unavailability of the reasoning behind an output, sometimes because the model is not interpretable and sometimes because the training data and its provenance are not disclosed; these are different problems with different remedies. Calibration within a group means that among those assigned the same score, the observed outcome rate matches the score. A false positive rate is the proportion of those who will not experience the outcome who are nonetheless selected; a false negative rate is the proportion of those who will who are not. Balance for the positive class requires equal false negative rates across groups, and balance for the negative class requires equal false positive rates. Contestability is the availability of a route by which an individual can effectively challenge an outcome, which requires more than the existence of an appeal form. A human in the loop is an official who can override the recommendation. The responsibility gap names the difficulty of attributing an outcome to any single agent when development, data collection, deployment, and case decision are distributed across parties. Prerequisite instruments: the legitimacy scope test from lesson 88, the two kinds of epistemic injustice from lesson 87, and the desert and responsibility distinctions of lesson 86.
depth.mechanism: Opacity damages legitimacy through a specific route, and it is worth stating precisely rather than gesturing at fairness. The service conception of lesson 88 justifies authority by the improvement in a subject’s conformity with the reasons that apply to her, and preemption is tolerable because the directive is meant to be based on those reasons. An opaque score breaks the link at the point of contestation: the subject is treated on grounds she cannot inspect, which prevents her from showing that the reasons applied to her were misapplied, and the burden of demonstrating error shifts to a party who cannot obtain the information. Epistemic injustice then compounds the harm, because a system trained on historical decisions reproduces the patterns those decisions contained, so the people most likely to be flagged are those whose records reflect earlier mistreatment, and their challenges arrive with a credibility handicap of the kind lesson 87 described. Two further mechanisms explain why remedies often fail. The first is deference by officials: a caseworker facing a recommendation and a heavy caseload tends to confirm it, which means a formal human in the loop may not restore the individualised judgment the legitimacy argument requires; this is an empirical claim about official behaviour that you should check in the literature rather than assume. The second is the responsibility gap: no single participant in a distributed decision can be held to have caused the outcome, so accountability structures that assume an identifiable decision-maker leave no one answerable. Against these, the case for using the instruments is serious and should be stated in its strongest form. Decisions are already being made by unaided humans whose judgments are inconsistent, opaque even to themselves, and demonstrably responsive to irrelevant factors, so the comparison is not between a flawed algorithm and an ideal human but between two imperfect processes. Whether the state should prefer the statistical instrument depends on comparative error rates and on whether contestability can be engineered, and that comparison is unsettled.
depth.secondExample: Apply the instruments to two deployments and notice that the answers differ because the dependent reasons differ. In the first, a court sets conditions of release using a risk score. The state is depriving a person of liberty, the subject has a direct and powerful interest in contesting the grounds, and the preemptive character of the decision is strong; on the legitimacy test, an opaque score used here must be accompanied by an individualised statement of reasons and a genuine opportunity to dispute the inputs, and if the score’s training data reflect arrest patterns rather than offending, the historical-pattern problem of lesson 87 makes the score’s apparent accuracy partly an artefact of past enforcement. In the second, an agency allocates routine inspections of food premises or lift safety using a risk score, and no individual is accused of anything, the burden is administrative, and the reasons that apply to the operators concern safety standards they are already bound by. Here the same model, with the same opacity, faces a weaker legitimacy objection because the subject can still show that her premises comply, and because the relevant error is an unnecessary inspection rather than a deprivation. The contrast yields a general rule for the capstone rather than a verdict about algorithms: identify the dependent reasons, the severity of the burden, and the availability of an alternative route to correct error, and let those determine whether opacity is disqualifying in that domain. A policy argument that treats all algorithmic governance as one thing will misclassify at least one of these cases.
depth.mistake: Three errors appear in the literature and in policy discussion. The first treats the trade-off among fairness criteria as a defect that more data or a better model will remove, when the result is structural and holds for a perfectly ranking predictor. The second treats opacity as disqualifying in general, without specifying the domain, the burden imposed, or the alternative, which makes the argument unavailable for the cases where it does decisive work. The third is the appeal to a human in the loop as a complete remedy, without evidence that the official actually exercises independent judgment; in institutions with volume targets, the loop is often a signature. Diagnostics: for any fairness claim, ask which criterion is satisfied and which is sacrificed; for any opacity claim, ask what the subject cannot do that she could do under an explainable process; for any accountability claim, ask which person is answerable for a specific outcome and what they could have done differently.
depth.application: Capstone task. Produce an analysis of one deployment, real or specified in detail, using eight labelled sections. (1) The question in one sentence, naming the decision-maker and the decision. (2) Three or more positions on whether the deployment is acceptable, each attributed to a literature or author from this level or its readings. (3) The legitimacy scope test from lesson 88: the dependent reasons, the improvement claimed, and the scope the justification supports. (4) One epistemic injustice finding from lesson 87, applied to the specific process. (5) The arithmetic: a stated base-rate difference and the error rates that follow under a stated selection rule, with the totals checked. (6) Your verdict with a confidence level. (7) One rebutting and one undercutting defeater. (8) What evidence would change your mind. Model response for a benefit-fraud detection model: (1) whether an agency may suspend benefits on the strength of an unexplained score before an interview; (2) positions: refusal, contestability, trade-off, transparency-first, with refusal drawing on the legitimacy argument and trade-off on the impossibility result; (3) dependent reasons are the interests of claimants in receiving what they are owed and of the public in accurate payment; the improvement claimed is fewer erroneous payments, and the scope supported is investigation of high-probability cases rather than suspension on a score alone, because suspension imposes the burden of the claimant’s error before it has been established; (4) claimants with records generated by earlier enforcement activity are systematically over-flagged, and their explanations meet a credibility deficit, an instance of the mechanism in lesson 87; (5) with base rates of 20 and 40 per cent in two groups of 100 and a rule flagging 30 in each, error rates are 12.5 and 0 per cent false positives and 0 and 25 per cent false negatives, and the totals remain 140 flagged across both groups; (6) verdict, suspension without individualised reasons is illegitimate, while investigation with reasons is defensible, at moderate confidence; (7) rebutting defeater: evidence that interview-based review restores accuracy, which would strengthen the case for the current practice; undercutting defeater: my knowledge of the agency’s internal guidance is second-hand; (8) I would change my view if a study showed that claimants who received reasons and a hearing had no greater success in correcting errors than those who did not. Rubric, six points: (1) the decision and the burden on the subject are named; (2) positions are attributed rather than invented; (3) the scope test produces a scope that is narrower or wider than the practice, or the section says why not; (4) the arithmetic is shown, conserved, and used to constrain the verdict rather than to decorate it; (5) the two defeaters are of different kinds and one concerns the writer’s own reasoning; (6) the confidence level and exit conditions are stated rather than implied.
depth.summary: The capstone combines the level’s instruments on a question that no single discipline resolves: what legitimacy requires when the state decides through predictions it cannot explain. The arithmetic of base rates tells you which choices are forced, the legitimacy test tells you which exercises of power need which justifications, and the analysis of epistemic injustice tells you whose histories are being scored. The verdict remains contested, and the defensible output is a position with its defeaters and its exit conditions attached rather than a claim that the question has been settled.

readings.title: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, ‘Ethics of Artificial Intelligence and Robotics’ — section 2.3, ‘Epistemic Issues: Opacity and Explainability’, and section 2.4, ‘Good Decisions: Fairness and Bias’
readings.note: Sections 2.3 and 2.4 survey the opacity and fairness debates in the form this capstone assumes, and section 2.7 covers responsibility. Read 2.3 first, since most arguments that appeal to explainability are really arguments about contested senses of opacity.

readings.title: Jon Kleinberg, Sendhil Mullainathan, and Manish Raghavan, ‘Inherent Trade-Offs in the Fair Determination of Risk Scores’ — arXiv preprint 1609.05807
readings.note: This is the source of the trade-off result used in the arithmetic. Read the informal introduction and the statement of the impossibility conditions rather than the proofs. It is a preprint that was subsequently published in a theory venue, so cite the paper and note that the impossibility holds under stated assumptions about the predictor and the base rates.

readings.title: Julia Angwin, Jeff Larson, Surya Mattu, and Lauren Kirchner, ‘Machine Bias’ (ProPublica, 2016), with the accompanying methodology article ‘How We Analyzed the COMPAS Recidivism Algorithm’
readings.note: Read both the investigation and its methodology page, then read a documented criticism of its analysis: the article’s central claims about disparate error rates were disputed by other researchers who argued that the instrument is calibrated. This is investigative journalism rather than peer-reviewed research, and the disagreement between the two analyses is itself the best illustration of the trade-off in the previous reading; treat none of the statistics as settled.

readings.title: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, ‘Computing and Moral Responsibility’ — section 1, ‘Challenges to Moral Responsibility’, and section 3, ‘Rethinking the Concept of Moral Responsibility’
readings.note: Section 1 sets out the causal contribution, consequence-based, and freedom-based challenges to attributing responsibility in computing contexts, and section 3 covers assigning responsibility and responsibility as a practice. Read it alongside the responsibility-gap discussion in this lesson.

readings.title: National Institute of Standards and Technology, ‘AI Risk Management Framework’ (NIST AI RMF 1.0)
readings.note: A voluntary federal framework rather than a philosophical source; useful for seeing which governance functions an institution commits to in practice, such as documenting intended use and measuring harm. Read the framework’s core functions and note what it does not do, namely settle which fairness criterion a system should satisfy.

visual.title: From an opaque score to a decision the state must justify
visual.description: Show the path from training data through a model to an individual decision, the points where opacity interrupts justification, and the two levers that policy can pull.
steps: Training data: historical decisions and enforcement patterns, including their past injustices
Model output: a score, with reasoning not available to the subject
Decision rule: threshold, human review, or automatic action, which determines the burden imposed
Break 1, epistemic: the subject cannot identify the grounds on which she was treated differently from a comparable person
Break 2, structural: officials defer to recommendations, so a formal human review may not restore individualised judgment
Lever A: choose and publicly justify an error distribution, since calibration and equal error rates cannot all hold when base rates differ
Lever B: restore contestability by stating reasons and providing an effective route to challenge the inputs, then measure whether challenges succeed

questions.prompt: A regulator is told that a surgeon’s exceptional earnings rest on a talent developed through training her family paid for, and that she works unusually long hours. Which argument bears most directly on whether she deserves her share?
questions.answer: The regress argument, since both the native endowment and the opportunity to develop it were unchosen, which threatens desert at its foundation rather than at the level of measurement
questions.distractor: The option-set objection, since the choiceworthiness of a position does not justify the range of positions available to the chooser
questions.correction: The option-set objection concerns choices made from unjustified alternatives; nothing in the scenario says her alternatives were defective. The regress argument is aimed at the desert base itself, and the scenario supplies exactly the unchosen inputs, family-funded training and unearned talent, that the argument cites.

questions.prompt: A housing authority accepts complaints only through an online form offering the grounds ‘noise’, ‘pest’, and ‘structural’. Residents want to report persistent damp that they attribute to a nearby excavation, and their submissions are returned as unclassifiable. Which injustice does the process display?
questions.answer: Hermeneutical injustice, since the shared categories cannot express what the residents are experiencing, so the failure lies in the interpretive resources rather than in any hearer’s prejudice
questions.distractor: Testimonial injustice, since the residents’ reports receive a credibility deficit attributable to prejudice against them as a group
questions.correction: No hearer’s credibility judgment is described here; the submissions are rejected by the categories themselves, and the rejection would fall on anyone whose concern did not map onto the listed grounds. That locates the wrong in the collective interpretive resources, which is Fricker’s second kind, and the remedy is a change in the categories rather than in the hearer’s virtue.

questions.prompt: A licensing scheme restricts entry to a trade, and the justification offered is that entrants should be inducted into the profession’s shared culture. Evaluate the authority claim.
questions.answer: The scope of the authority exceeds the justification, and the appeal to a shared culture raises the neutrality objection, since conformity with the reasons that already apply to entrants does not require the culture
questions.distractor: The scheme lacks authority for all entrants, since any restriction on entry requires the consent of those it excludes
questions.correction: A competence-based licensing scheme can satisfy the normal justification, so the objection cannot be that entry restrictions never have authority. What fails here is the particular justification, which reaches beyond competence to a contested conception of the good, and that is both a scope failure and a neutrality failure.

questions.prompt: Two colleagues equal in evidence and competence disagree about a technical question. One of them subsequently notices a procedural error in her own reasoning that does not alter the substantive data on either side. What follows?
questions.answer: An undercutting defeater has appeared, so confidence should fall until she can estimate the error’s effect, even though no counter-argument was offered against her conclusion
questions.distractor: The disagreement is now settled in her colleague’s favour, since an acknowledged procedural error shows that her conclusion was false
questions.correction: Undercutting defeaters bear on the grounds of a belief rather than on its truth, which is why a procedural flaw can damage justification without refuting the conclusion, and conversely a conclusion can be true while its support is undermined. The correction is to reduce confidence and investigate the error’s magnitude, not to transfer the verdict to the other party.

questions.prompt: A ministry requires a risk-scoring instrument to be calibrated within each affected group and to have equal false positive rates, and the vendor promises that a larger and more representative dataset will deliver both, although the groups have different base rates for the outcome. Evaluate the promise.
questions.answer: The trade-off is structural, so no dataset will deliver both conditions when the base rates differ, and the requirement must be revised to state which criterion is chosen and why
questions.distractor: The trade-off reflects data quality, so a larger and more representative sample will normally allow both conditions to hold at once
questions.correction: The impossibility result holds for predictors that rank perfectly, so it cannot be repaired by adding data; what varies with data quality is how well the instrument predicts, not whether calibration and equal error rates can coexist under unequal base rates. The policy question is which error distribution is to be preferred, and that is a legitimacy question rather than a statistical one.

questions.prompt: A tribunal reasons that a claimant cannot be a reliable witness to her own past because her self-account has changed over the years and she refuses to narrate the earlier period as her own. Diagnose the reasoning with the tools of this level.
questions.answer: It converts an ideal of narrativity into a test of identity while imposing a credibility deficit on the claimant for failing to produce the self-account the tribunal expects, which are two separate errors with separate remedies
questions.distractor: It assumes that personal identity comes in degrees and that the claimant’s account is fictional rather than merely selective
questions.correction: Neither identity coming in degrees nor fiction is at issue. The first error is the identity claim, which treats the failure to satisfy the reality and endorsement constraints as a change of person; the second is epistemic, since the discounting is driven by what the account is expected to look like rather than by evidence about this claimant’s reliability.

questions.prompt: A student argues, first, that because no amount of physical detail entails experience, dualism is established, and second, that because a functionally identical duplicate without experience can be conceived, such a duplicate is possible. Assess both steps.
questions.answer: Each step converts an epistemic gap into a metaphysical conclusion, and each therefore needs an additional premise linking what can be conceived or explained to what exists
questions.distractor: Neither step needs further support, since the conceivability of a duplicate that is physically identical to a conscious being entails its possibility
questions.correction: The first step moves from a failure of deduction to a claim about what exists, which is precisely the reading the phenomenal-concept strategy resists. The second moves from conceivability to possibility, and that inference is the contested hinge rather than a self-evident truth. Both arguments are therefore conditional on a premise that the disputants deny.

questions.prompt: An agent acts from her own settled reasons after deliberating as she normally does, and a device stands ready to compel her if she had wavered, so that she could not have acted otherwise. A colleague argues that blame is therefore misplaced. Evaluate.
questions.answer: The colleague makes the leeway condition necessary for responsibility, which the sourcehood cases challenge, since the action flowed from the agent’s own reasons and the alternative was never needed
questions.distractor: The colleague is right, because responsibility requires that the agent could have done otherwise in the situation, so any blocked alternative exculpates
questions.correction: The example is constructed so that the counterfactual intervention never operates, and the agent deliberates and acts on her own reasons throughout. Making the ability to do otherwise necessary would exculpate her, which is the result the sourcehood tradition treats as the argument’s reductio rather than its conclusion.

questions.prompt: A legislator argues that people should bear the costs of their own bad choices and that unchosen disadvantages should be equalised. Which two objections from this level most directly threaten the position?
questions.answer: The regress objection, since the capacity to choose well is itself a product of unchosen conditions, and the option-set objection, since a choice made from an unjustified range of alternatives does not settle the justice of the outcome
questions.distractor: The desert objection, since only contributions can ground a claim to a share, and the sufficiency objection, since only a floor matters
questions.correction: Desert and sufficiency are rival criteria rather than objections internal to the legislator’s view. The two arguments that attack the position on its own terms are the regress, which undermines the responsibility it tracks, and the option-set point, which denies that choice can be assessed before the alternatives are assessed.

questions.prompt: Consider two flawed arguments. The first treats a threat of punishment as though it showed that the threatened person has an admirable character. The second attributes to an opponent a crude version of a view the opponent states with qualifications. Name the diagnosis for each.
questions.answer: The first has a wrong-kind-of-reason problem, since the incentive bears on holding the attitude rather than on the object, and the second fails the principle of charity
questions.distractor: The first commits the internalist fallacy by ignoring the agent’s motivational set, and the second is a reductio of the opponent’s position
questions.correction: Internalism is a thesis about what makes a consideration a reason, not a fallacy, and misrepresenting an opponent is not a reductio, which is a valid argument form used to show that a view entails an unacceptable consequence. The diagnoses are the wrong kind of reason and the failure of charity, which are separate faults.

questions.prompt: A state justifies a compulsory biometric registry by appeal to administrative efficiency in benefits and taxation. Residents in one district object that their records have repeatedly been wrong and that the objection procedure requires them to prove a negative. Assess the justification and the objection.
questions.answer: The efficiency claim supports authority over the administrative domain it improves, while the objection identifies a credibility and interpretive failure that the efficiency argument does not answer, so the two claims must be met separately
questions.distractor: The efficiency claim justifies the registry in every domain it touches, because administrative reasons preempt individual judgment wherever the state acts
questions.correction: Preemption is licensed only by the justification that generates it, so efficiency in tax and benefits supports the registry in those functions and not elsewhere. The residents’ objection is independent: repeated record errors and a procedure requiring proof of a denial raise a credibility deficit and a contestability problem that improved administration does not by itself remedy.

questions.prompt: Which claim about authority can a philosophical anarchist accept along with a defender of the service conception?
questions.answer: That an exercise of power may be justified with respect to those subject to it without any particular person having a standing obligation to obey it
questions.distractor: That a justified state has a general claim on the obedience of everyone within its territory, which anarchism denies only for unjust states
questions.correction: Separating legitimacy from obligation is what allows the two positions to share ground: the anarchist denies the personal bond while allowing that power may be justified, and nothing in the service conception requires the bond either, since it grounds authority in improved conformity with reasons rather than in an act of acceptance.

questions.prompt: A position dossier states a verdict at moderate confidence and lists one counter-argument. It includes no assessment of the author’s own reasoning and no statement of what would change her mind. What is missing, and why does it matter?
questions.answer: It omits higher-order evidence about the reliability of the author’s own reasoning and omits the exit condition, so the dossier cannot be assessed for responsiveness to evidence and cannot be audited later
questions.distractor: Nothing material is missing, since a verdict and a counter-argument are jointly sufficient for a contested question
questions.correction: A counter-argument is a rebutting defeater, which is only one of the two kinds. Undercutting defeaters bear on the grounds of the writer’s own reasoning, and without an exit condition the reader cannot tell whether the position is held on evidence or on attachment, which is the difference between steadfastness and obstinacy.

questions.prompt: Which pair of claims should a capstone defend about the tension among group-wise calibration, equal false positive rates, and equal false negative rates?
questions.answer: That the tension is a structural property of predictors when base rates differ, and that the resulting choice among error distributions must be stated and justified by a legitimacy argument
questions.distractor: That the tension is an artefact of incomplete data, and that a sufficiently large sample removes the need to choose among the criteria
questions.correction: The result holds even for a predictor that ranks every case correctly, so it cannot be removed by adding data. The genuinely contested question is which error distribution the state may impose on which population and in which domain, and that question is answered, if at all, by the justification of the authority rather than by the mathematics.

questions.prompt: An agent’s entire self-understanding, including the narrative she tells about her commitments, was installed by others before she could evaluate it. She now acts on it deliberately. How do the manipulation argument and the narrative view bear on this case?
questions.answer: They pull in different directions: the manipulation argument treats the installed origin as bearing on responsibility, while the narrative view asks whether the story satisfies the reality constraint and is one she can inhabit, so an installed story can be a real self-understanding even when its origin is rigged
questions.distractor: They are independent, since narrativity concerns self-understanding while manipulation concerns causation, and no question about origin can bear on either
questions.correction: Both frameworks ask about the connection between an agent and the sources of her conduct, so they cannot be treated as independent. Their estrangement over the installed narrative is instructive: the origin is exactly what the manipulation argument presses on, while the narrative view can accommodate it provided the reality and endorsement constraints are met, which shows that the responsibility question is not settled by the story alone.

questions.prompt: An agency accepts the output of an opaque predictive model as though it were testimony from a competent source, and denies any wrong on the ground that a program is not a person. Assess that reasoning.
questions.answer: The reasoning mistakes the locus of the wrong: the injustice falls on the people whose grounds cannot be examined and contested, and treating the model as a testifier shifts the burden onto subjects who cannot discharge it
questions.distractor: The reasoning is sound, since epistemic injustice requires a prejudiced human hearer and therefore cannot arise from a purely mechanical process
questions.correction: Testimonial injustice requires a human hearer, but the analysis does not stop at the hearer: it concerns whose accounts are believed and who bears the burden of correction in a process. An opaque score compounds the historic credibility problems of the people who are most often flagged, and the remedy is contestability by design rather than an appeal to the model’s non-personhood.

questions.prompt: Once the arithmetic of base rates has fixed the menu of error distributions available to a policy, what remains to be decided, and by what argument?
questions.answer: Which distribution may be imposed on which population and in which domain, decided by the justification of the state’s authority rather than by the arithmetic
questions.distractor: Which criterion minimises total error, since the legitimate criterion is by definition the one with the smallest aggregate error
questions.correction: The arithmetic constrains the options and settles nothing about permission, since minimising aggregate error can distribute burdens unjustly across groups and imposes different costs on different people. The remaining question is normative: which error may the state impose, on whom, in pursuit of which dependent reasons, and that is a legitimacy question of the kind lesson 88 sets out.
